title: Show HN: I put employees inside S&P 500 market-cap bubbles
author: vfxGer
body:
Big Whale Hunting: Market Cap vs. Employees , 
× 
Each bubble is an S&P 500 company, its area proportional to its market capitalization
 as of , grouped by sector.
 Inside it, one stick figure stands for employees, so a bubble crowded with
 small figures is worth little per worker and a big bubble with a handful of figures is worth a lot.
 Every figure is the same size, so how densely a bubble is filled shows its employees per dollar of market cap.
Only companies with at least employees and a market cap of at least
 are shown ( of the S&P 500), plus a few
 big companies with fewer employees, such as Palantir and Welltower, drawn as one half-size figure.
 Employee counts are full-time staff from each company's latest annual report, so they lag up to a year.
 Click a company for its details; scroll or pinch to zoom in on the small ones.

comments.author: drewlem
comments.text: Have spent the last 20 years building and launching software in some of the biggest companies in the world. Every week I hear people debating "build vs. buy" or someone bragging about how much money they saved building custom tech in house.I think we are going into a 2027 that will be somehow even more confusing than 2026, and I wanted a place that had more data and facts and less opinions. Hopefully over time we can aggregate enough real data to build consensus.The data comes from real people, real posts, listings from builders, and sourced stories. While one of them alone might exaggerate the truth, over time it will be obvious when you average out the data.Just getting going with this, so would love feedback. And if you are building your own platforms, or have data to add, feel free to add it. In some places data is still thin, but I'm adding more to it each day.Thanks for your help in getting more data out there and less opinions on the whole "build vs. buy" conversation when it comes to software platforms.

title: Show HN: Kolo – share your AI coding sessions with anyone
author: whosgotch
body:
# komovaar/kolo

Multiplayer AI coding agents. One machine runs them, everybody else opens a link. 

- Stars: 7
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 7
- Open issues: 0
- License: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-08-11T19:53:09Z

## Languages

- CSS
- Go
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- komovaar (380 contributions)
- codex (5 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 Kolo
 

**Multiplayer AI coding agents.**

Run agents on one machine and work together in the browser. Share a link so your
team can watch, type, and take over the same session. Only the host installs Kolo.

CI
Release
License: AGPL-3.0

A shared Codex session in Kolo, with sessions grouped by machine and project

## Why Kolo

- **Work in the same session.** Everyone sees the same terminal. Type a prompt,
 approve a step, or pick up where a teammate left off.
- **Bring your terminal agents.** Built-in adapters for Claude Code, Codex CLI,
 and opencode, with custom agent descriptions for other tools.
- **Give observers a seat.** Read-only members can follow along while the host
 decides who can control sessions.

## Quick start

Kolo is an experimental alpha for trusted teams. Agents run with the host user's
permissions. Start in a dedicated VM with only the projects and credentials you
intend to share; see the isolation setup.

Install on the machine that will run the agents:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/komovaar/kolo/main/install | KOLO_VERSION=v0.1.0 sh
```

Then open a project and start Kolo:

```sh
cd /path/to/project
kolo up
```

Send your team the invitation link printed in the terminal. They open it in a
browser, choose a name, and join. No install or token to paste.

Hosts support Linux and macOS on amd64 and arm64. Use WSL2 on Windows.
For rolling development builds, replace `v0.1.0` with `nightly`.

## How it works

One Go binary runs the hub your team opens and the host that starts agents.
`kolo up` runs both together. Use `kolo serve` and `kolo host` to run them on
separate machines. Hosts connect out to the hub; the hub needs to be reachable
from your team's browsers.

Kolo detects agent status from terminal output, so CLI updates can affect status
and resume behavior. Run `kolo doctor` to check your setup, and see
tested versions and limits for current compatibility.

## Documentation

Start with `kolo help` or `kolo help `.

# This Open-Source Cybersecurity Platform Uses AI Agents to Detect Threats and Protect Businesses Automatically

Thomas Unise

Hey everyone , I built ARGUS, a free, open-source cybersecurity platform designed to help businesses find security threats, investigate attacks, and respond to them automatically.

I wanted to build something that could handle much of the work a cybersecurity team normally does, using AI agents, without giving up control over what actions get taken.

Here’s what it actually does:

- 24/7 security monitoring: Watches your servers, cloud infrastructure, networks, employee accounts, devices, and code for suspicious activity.
- * Threat detection: Identifies unusual logins, security vulnerabilities, potential attacks, and other signs that something is wrong.
- * AI investigations: Uses seven specialized AI agents to investigate alerts, review evidence, identify potential threats, and recommend what to do.
- * Automated protection: Can block suspicious IP addresses, isolate compromised devices, and take other protective actions. You decide which actions can happen automatically and which require approval.
- * Security testing: Tests your authorized systems for vulnerabilities and weaknesses before someone else finds them.
- * AI security: Detects unauthorized AI tools and suspicious AI agent activity. It also includes tools to test whether your systems can detect attacks involving AI agents.
- * Security reporting: Records security events, investigations, approvals, and actions. Includes support for common security compliance frameworks.

It also integrates with services like AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, GitHub, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, and others.

A few other things worth mentioning:

You can host it on your own infrastructure, use OpenAI, Anthropic, or locally hosted models, and decide exactly how much access and autonomy you want to give it.

The automated response features are disabled by default, and there are approval requirements, safety limits, and rollback controls.

It’s released under the MIT license, so anyone can use it, modify it, or contribute to its development.

I built ARGUS because I think businesses should have access to better cybersecurity tools without needing an enormous security budget.

It’s available on GitHub now. I’d love to get feedback from developers, security engineers, and anyone interested in trying it.

https://github.com/thomasunise/argus

title: Show HN: Farol – a risk map of a pull request for the person who approves it
author: ericholiveira
body:
# winnin/farol

Know the risk of merging a pull request, and where it lives. Free, open-source CLI and GitHub Action: after your AI review, farol shows the riskiest files, what they reach, diff coverage and contract breaks. TypeScript/React, Go, Python.

- Stars: 3
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 3
- Open issues: 5
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: https://winnin.github.io/farol/
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-21T21:52:58Z

## Languages

- Go
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Python
- TypeScript

## Topics

- ai-code-review
- cli
- code-review
- developer-tools
- diff-coverage
- fastapi
- github-actions
- golang
- nextjs
- pull-requests
- python
- react
- risk-analysis
- static-analysis
- typescript

## Top Contributors

- erich-oliveira-winnin (9 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 

 Know the risk of merging a pull request, and where it lives. 

 
 A free, open-source CLI and GitHub Action. After your AI review, farol tells the person who approves how risky the
 merge is and which files carry the risk, so the riskiest changes get the most attention.
 

 
 Website ·
 Live demo ·
 Get started ·
 Reference 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

---

Agents write the code and agents review it. The last call is still a person's: approve the merge or not. That
approval is the scarce part, and spread evenly over every pull request it turns into a skim, which is how a one-line
change to a shared hook takes down forty pages.

**farol comes after the AI review, not instead of it.** Your review agent comments on the lines in the diff. farol
gives the person who approves what the agent cannot reliably give: **the risk of accepting the change, and where it
lives**. The goal is not only a faster review: low-risk pull requests can go fast, and the risky ones get read line by
line, starting with the files that carry the risk. It works from static analysis (the compilers' own view of your
code, not a model's guess), so the same pull request always gets the same answer.

The Claude Code team describes the same principle in
How the Claude Code team does code review: review effort
follows the risk of the change. As they put it, "The change sets the tier, not the author."

**farol** (Portuguese for *lighthouse*) does the triage before the reviewer opens the diff:

- **What does this change reach?** Every existing page, API operation, RPC method, job and script that runs the changed code, with the call chain to each.
- **How risky is the merge?** A verdict (*fast track*, *quick review*, *careful review*) and a 0–100 risk score from reach, diff coverage, security findings, contract breaks and dependency changes.
- **Where do I start?** The riskiest files first, with inline diffs, untested lines marked, and a checklist of what to try by hand.

**Free and open source (MIT).** Run it as a CLI with `npx @winninjs/farol`, or on every pull request with the GitHub
Action `winnin/farol/action`. No account, no hosted service: it runs on your machine or in your CI runner, comments on
every PR and never blocks a merge. It **never executes your code** and never sends it anywhere.

 
 
 
 
 
 

## Live demo

**See farol on a real pull request →**

The demo holds the reports farol produced in CI for a pull request on the
FastAPI full-stack template: a FastAPI backend and a React
frontend with TanStack Router. The pull request adds a status to items and an Insights page, with the kind of problems
a reviewer should catch: a breaking API change, SQL built with an f-string, a shared component without tests.

- Backend report: ⚠ careful review, a breaking contract change and a high-severity security finding.
- Frontend report: ⚠ careful review, a new page and the existing pages a shared component reaches.

The reports are interactive: mark files as reviewed, mark a page as behind a feature flag, open the inline diffs,
follow the test plan and copy the review record from the Result tab. They are the same files the pull request's
comments link to (the pull request); the
copies live in `docs/demo/`.

## farol after your AI review

| | AI review agents | farol |
|---|---|---|
| **Reads** | the diff, and whatever context fits in the prompt | the whole program at the base and the head, with the compilers (TypeScript type checker, `go/types`, Python `ast`) |
| **Tells you** | what may be wrong in these lines | what these lines reach, how risky the merge is, and where to look first |
| **Answers are** | probabilistic: worded differently on every run | deterministic: the same PR gives the same report, and every claim comes with its call chain |
| **When unsure** | may sound confident anyway | says `unknown` and asks for a careful review |
| **Runs** | a model, usually a hosted service | locally or in your CI: it never executes your code and never sends it anywhere |

Use both, in that order. The agent reviews the lines first; then farol tells the person who approves how much attention
the merge needs, which files deserve it, which pages and endpoints to test by hand and which contract changes need
their clients checked. The agent's review is not enough exactly when a small change has a large reach, and that is
what farol shows.

## Why farol

- **Review attention goes where the risk is.** A 40-file PR usually has two or three files that can actually hurt. farol ranks them, so the reviewer reads those closely and skims the rest with a clear conscience.
- **It follows the code, not the file names.** farol builds a declaration graph with the real compilers (the TypeScript type checker, `go/types`, Python's `ast`). A change to `formatPrice` lists the twelve pages that render it, not "1 file changed".
- **Contract breaks are caught before clients are.** Removed response fields, new required parameters, changed types in GraphQL, FastAPI, Go handlers and gRPC, with the services that call each endpoint.
- **Review the whole PR, or just what changed since your last look.** Every push gets two reports: the full pull request, and only the commits since the previous push. After a round of fixes, the reviewer checks the new commits instead of starting over.
- **It uses what your CI already has.** Coverage, lint, security and audit reports become diff coverage and findings on the changed lines. Nothing runs twice.
- **Fail closed.** When farol cannot read part of a change, it says so (`unknown`) and asks for a careful review. It never calls something safe because it did not understand it.
- **Built for the human in the loop.** Mark files as reviewed, mark pages as behind a feature flag, check off findings, and paste the result back in the PR as a record of what was reviewed.

## Contents

- Live demo
- farol after your AI review
- Get started
- Recipes: React Router · Next.js · TanStack Router · TypeScript API · Go · Python · Datadog
- What is supported
- Reading the review
- How it works · Security · Limitations · FAQ
- Reference (every command, option and configuration key)

## Get started

You need **Node.js 22+** and **git** (plus `go` for Go projects, `python3` 3.11+ for Python ones). Nothing to
install: run farol with `npx @winninjs/farol`.

**1. Describe your project** in a `farol.config.json` at its root. One line is enough to start; pick your stack:

| Your project | `farol.config.json` | Full recipe |
|---|---|---|
| React app with React Router | `{ "routes": { "file": "src/routes.tsx" } }` (the file that builds the route table) | React Router |
| Next.js app (Pages or App Router) | `{ "routes": { "adapter": "next" } }` | Next.js |
| React app with TanStack Router | `{ "routes": { "adapter": "tanstack-router", "dir": "src/routes" } }` | TanStack Router |
| TypeScript API (GraphQL, REST) | `{ "surface": "backend" }` | TypeScript API |
| Go service | `{ "language": "go", "surface": "backend" }` | Go |
| Python service (FastAPI, Flask, Django, Celery…) | `{ "language": "python", "surface": "backend" }` | Python |

**2. Check what farol sees:** the pages, endpoints, jobs and scripts it found.

```sh
npx @winninjs/farol routes
```

**3. Analyze a branch** against its target and open the report.

```sh
npx @winninjs/farol analyze --base origin/main --head HEAD --out farol.json
npx @winninjs/farol html --in farol.json --out farol.html && open farol.html     # xdg-open on Linux
```

### Example: a React app with React Router

```sh
cd path/to/your/react-app
echo '{ "routes": { "file": "src/routes.tsx" } }' > farol.config.json

npx @winninjs/farol routes                                        # lists your pages: "/", "/products", "/settings"…
git checkout my-feature-branch
npx @winninjs/farol analyze --base origin/main --head HEAD --out farol.json
npx @winninjs/farol html --in farol.json --out farol.html && open farol.html
```

The report already shows the verdict, the score, the files to start with, the pages the change reaches and what to
test by hand. **Next steps:** add your coverage, lint and audit reports and run farol on every PR with the
recipe for your stack. Every option is in the reference and, per stack, in
examples/README.md.

> Running it often? `npm install --global @winninjs/farol` gives you a plain `farol` command.

## Recipes

Each recipe has three parts: the `farol.config.json` to commit, the reports to produce, and the GitHub Actions
workflow. The workflows in `examples/` are complete and share one shape:

1. **`tests`** runs your tests, linter and audit and keeps the reports. It runs the PR's code, so it has no secrets and a read-only token. If you already have a test job, keep it and add its upload step.
2. **`farol`** runs after it (pass or fail), reads git and the reports, and posts a **new comment on every push** with a link that opens the HTML report in the browser, plus a second report with only the commits since the previous push. It never runs the PR's code.
3. Drafts are skipped, fork PRs get no comment (their token is read-only), and every farol step is `continue-on-error`.

Pin the action to a commit once it works for you: `winnin/farol/action@ # main as of `.

`examples/README.md` goes deeper for each stack: every configuration key, CLI parameter and
action input, and how to check a setup.

### React frontend (React Router)

React Router route tables (object and JSX forms, lazy routes, split route modules), reach per declaration.

```json
{
  "routes": { "file": "src/routes.tsx" },
  "roles": { "global": ["src/main.tsx", "src/App.tsx", "src/styles/global.css", "package.json", "vite.config.ts"] }
}
```

```sh
npx vitest run --coverage.enabled --coverage.reporter=json --coverage.reportsDirectory=reports/coverage
npx eslint -f json -o reports/eslint.json <changed files>
npm audit --json > reports/audit.json                     # or pnpm audit --json

npx @winninjs/farol analyze --base origin/main --head HEAD \
  --coverage reports/coverage/coverage-final.json --eslint reports/eslint.json --audit reports/audit.json --out farol.json
```

**CI:** copy `examples/workflow.yml` to `.github/workflows/farol.yml`.

Set `coverage.include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}']` in the Vitest config so files no test loads are reported as untested.
Split route trees go in `routes.extraFiles`; a fuller config is in examples/farol.config.json.

### Next.js

Pages Router and App Router: every page, API route, layout, `_app`/`_document` and middleware, read from the file
names. Dynamic segments (`[id]`), catch-alls, route groups and parallel slots are understood.

```json
{
  "routes": { "adapter": "next" },
  "roles": { "global": ["next.config.*", "package.json"] }
}
```

`pages/` and `app/` are found in the project or in its `src/`; set `"dir"` when they live elsewhere. Reports and CI
are the same as for React Router (Jest or Vitest coverage, ESLint, audit). In a
monorepo whose tsconfig extends a workspace package (`"extends": "tsconfig/nextjs.json"`), install dependencies
before analyzing, so the package is in `node_modules`.

### TanStack Router

File-based routing: every module calling `createFileRoute(' ')` under the routes directory, with the root route,
pathless layouts (`_app`) and parent routes as layouts of their children.

```json
{ "routes": { "adapter": "tanstack-router", "dir": "src/routes" } }
```

Reports and CI are the same as for React Router.

### TypeScript API (GraphQL or REST)

GraphQL root operations (schema files and `gql` templates, per resolver) and Fastify/Express-style REST endpoints.

```json
{
  "surface": "backend",
  "backend": { "graphql": true, "rest": true },
  "roles": { "global": ["package.json", "src/app.ts"] }
}
```

Reports and CI are the same as for React Router: `examples/workflow.yml`. If
resolvers reach data through an injected context (`ctx.loaders.Brand.byId()`), tell farol where the providers live:
`"backend": { "context": { "loaders": ["src/modules/*/loaders/index.ts"] } }`.

### Go service

chi, gin, echo and net/http routes, gRPC service methods and `main` binaries, reach per declaration with interface
calls resolved to their implementations.

```json
{ "language": "go", "surface": "backend" }
```

```sh
go test -coverpkg=./... -coverprofile=reports/cover.out ./...
golangci-lint run --output.json.path=reports/golangci.json --issues-exit-code=0 ./...   # enable gosec
govulncheck -json ./... > reports/govulncheck.json

npx @winninjs/farol analyze --base origin/main --head HEAD \
  --coverage reports/cover.out --eslint reports/golangci.json --audit reports/govulncheck.json --out farol.json
```

**CI:** copy `examples/workflow-go.yml`. farol reads modules offline, so the workflow runs
`go mod download` for the base and the head first.

### Python service

FastAPI and Flask routes (routers, blueprints, prefixes), Django URLs, MCP tools/resources/prompts, Celery tasks,
Temporal workflows and activities, Prefect flows and `__main__` scripts. farol parses your code; it never imports it.

```json
{ "language": "python", "surface": "backend", "python": { "roots": ["src", "."] } }
```

```sh
pytest --cov=src --cov-report=json:reports/coverage.json
ruff check --output-format json --extend-select S --exit-zero . > reports/ruff.json    # S = flake8-bandit
pip-audit --format json -o reports/pip-audit.json

npx @winninjs/farol analyze --base origin/main --head HEAD \
  --coverage reports/coverage.json --eslint reports/ruff.json --audit reports/pip-audit.json --out farol.json
```

**CI:** copy `examples/workflow-python.yml` (uses `uv`; swap in your installer).

### Add Datadog traffic and errors

Optional, and information only: it never changes the score. With it the report shows how much traffic each affected
page or operation gets, its **distinct production errors** (linked to Datadog), the changed files that already throw
errors, and the services that call each changed endpoint.

```json
{
  "datadog": {
    "env": "prod",
    "rum": { "applicationId": "<RUM application id>" },
    "apm": { "service": "orders-api", "operations": ["fastapi.request"] }
  }
}
```

```sh
DD_API_KEY=… DD_APP_KEY=… npx @winninjs/farol usage --out usage.json      # last 14 days
npx @winninjs/farol analyze … --usage usage.json
```

**CI:** the example workflows have a `farol-usage` job: set the `DD_API_KEY` and `DD_APP_KEY` secrets and the
repository variable `FAROL_DATADOG=true`. It reads Datadog once a day and never sees the PR's code. Keys, scopes and
matching rules are in the reference.

## What is supported

| | TypeScript / React frontends | TypeScript / JavaScript backends | Go | Python |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Entry points** | React Router route tables (object and JSX forms, lazy routes, split route modules); Next.js Pages and App Router (pages, API routes, layouts, middleware); TanStack Router file-based routes | GraphQL root operations (schema files and `gql` templates) and REST endpoints (Fastify/Express style) | chi, gin, echo and net/http routes; gRPC service methods; `main` binaries | FastAPI and Flask routes (routers, blueprints, prefixes); Django URLs; MCP tools, resources and prompts; Celery tasks; Temporal workflows and activities; Prefect flows; `__main__` scripts |
| **Reach precision** | per declaration (TypeScript type checker) | per module, per resolver for GraphQL | per declaration (`go/types`, interface calls resolved to implementations) | per declaration (Python `ast` with local type inference) |
| **Contract changes** | — | GraphQL schema (breaking / dangerous / safe) | Handler request and response types (net/http, chi, gin, echo); gRPC messages | FastAPI parameters, body, response and Pydantic models |
| **Dependencies** | `package.json` + npm/pnpm/yarn/bun lockfiles | same | `go.mod` + `go.sum` | `pyproject.toml` (PEP 621, extras, groups, uv, Poetry), `requirements.txt` + `uv.lock`/`poetry.lock`/`Pipfile.lock` |
| **Diff coverage** | Istanbul `coverage-final.json` (Vitest, Jest) | same | `go test -coverprofile` | coverage.py JSON (`pytest --cov`) |
| **Lint** | `eslint -f json` | same | golangci-lint JSON | ruff JSON |
| **Security** | built-in rules (XSS sinks, `eval`, hard-coded secrets, `javascript:` URLs…) | same | gosec (through golangci-lint) | flake8-bandit (ruff `S` rules) |
| **Vulnerabilities** | `npm audit --json`, `pnpm audit --json` | same | `govulncheck -json` | `pip-audit --format json` |
| **Suppressions** | `eslint-disable`, `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-expect-error`, `as any`… | same | `//nolint`, `//lint:ignore`, `#nosec` | `# noqa`, `# type: ignore`, `# nosec`, `# pragma: no cover`… |
| **Traffic and errors** (optional) | Datadog RUM page views and errors | Datadog APM requests, error spans and callers | same | same |

In every language: environment, infrastructure and CI files (`.env*`, Dockerfiles, compose, CI pipelines, helm, k8s,
terraform…) in a section of their own; incremental analysis since any commit (`--since`); suggested reviewers from
git blame and CODEOWNERS; reports as a GitHub comment, Markdown or a single-file HTML page.

## Reading the review

farol produces two things: a **PR comment** with the verdict, the top files and a test checklist, and a
**single-file HTML report** (linked from the comment) where the review happens. Here is what each part is for and how
to use it.

### Verdict and merge risk score

What it tells you is how much of your time the PR deserves.

| Verdict | Means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| ✓ **Fast track** | Only new code, tests or low-risk changes. | Skim the diff and approve. |
| ◐ **Quick review** | Existing code changed in a contained way, or a weaker signal (low coverage, lint errors, a config file). | Check the *Start here* files, then approve. |
| ⚠ **Careful review** | Wide or silent breakage is possible: a score of 60+, a breaking contract change, a high-severity finding, an untested central file, or code farol could not read. | Read the *Start here* files line by line and test what they reach. |

The **score** (0–100) is the chance that at least one risky item breaks something. Expand *What adds to it* to see
each item and its points: the files by reach × untested share, findings, contract changes, dependencies. The verdict
always comes with its reasons; read them before the diff.

### Start here

The changed code files, riskiest first. Each row shows how many existing pages or operations run the file, its diff
coverage, its findings and its own risk points; with Datadog, also its traffic and production errors. Open the inline
diff: added lines no test runs are marked **○**, lines with findings **⚠**.

**How to use it:** review top-down and tick **Mark as reviewed** on each file. The score drops as you go, so you
always know how much risk is left. Below it come the low-risk files to skim, environment/infrastructure/CI files
(check their values per environment), and files that need no review (docs, lockfiles, tests).

### Behind a feature flag

On every page or operation row, and in a panel at the top: mark an entry point that is entirely behind a flag. Files
that **only** flagged entry points use leave the review, labeled *behind a flag* rather than reviewed. Use it for
work-in-progress features shipped dark, so the remaining score reflects what users will actually hit.

### Pages / Operations

Every new and affected entry point, as a list or a tree by module. Opening one draws **how** the change reaches it,
file by file. With Datadog each one shows its traffic share and its distinct errors, busiest first. **Use it** to
judge blast radius: a change reaching 3 rarely used admin pages is not the same as one reaching the checkout.

### Contracts (backends)

Each endpoint whose request or response shape changed, as **breaking** (clients built for the base can fail),
**dangerous** (they may misbehave) or **safe** (compatible additions), with the exact field and the calling services
from Datadog. **Use it** to confirm every breaking change is intended and its clients are updated, then tick
*checked with clients*.

 

### Security, Dependencies, Coverage

The evidence behind the score: security findings on the changed lines (with a *checked* box each), added or bumped
dependencies with known vulnerabilities, and diff coverage per file. A report that was not given shows as
**not verified**, never as passing.

### Test plan

The new and affected pages or operations to try by hand, new ones first, then by the risk of the file that reaches
them. The PR comment has it as a task list. **Use it** when you run the branch locally or on a preview environment.
It follows your review: once every changed file behind an item is marked as reviewed, the item is marked too
(✓ files reviewed), or 🚩 behind a flag. Its own checkbox, for the manual test, stays yours to tick.

### Reviewers

Who should review: the people who wrote the code this PR changes (git blame, weighted by each file's risk), plus
CODEOWNERS. The PR's own authors and bots are left out, and inactive people are labeled. **Use it** to request the
person who knows the riskiest file, not just whoever is free.

### Result

A Markdown record of the review: the initial verdict and score, the score left now, the flagged entry points, the
reviewed files, and the checked findings and contract changes. **Copy as Markdown** and paste it in the PR as your
review comment, so the next person knows what was looked at.

### Since the last push

After a push to an open PR, the comment carries a second report with only the commits since the previous push
(`analyze --since `; after a force-push, from its merge-base). Its verdict, score and *Start here* cover just
those changes. **Use it** for the second round of a review: check that the fixes do what was asked and nothing
else, then go back to the full report only if the new commits reach somewhere new.

### Class and reasons

Kept in *Details* and a collapsed block of the comment, so reviewers form their own opinion first:
`isolated` (only adds), `touches-existing` (existing code changed), `global` (a global file, manifest or critical
dependency) and `unknown` (part of the change could not be read: never safe). Every reason code is in
docs/reasons.md.

## How it works

1. **Diff** the merge-base and the head, detecting renames and ignoring whitespace-only and trailing-comma lines.
2. **Read both trees without running anything**: the TypeScript compiler API, `go list` + `go/types` (offline), Python `ast`. From them, the entry points and a graph of which declaration uses which.
3. **Compare declarations** by a hash of their code, so comments and formatting never count. New declarations and entry points are additive.
4. **Reach**: from each changed declaration to every entry point that runs it, keeping the shortest chain.
5. **Classify, weigh and plan**: class, score, verdict, files to start with, test checklist.

On 662 past commits of four repositories, *fast track* had **0 problems in 56 commits** and the score's AUC was
**0.72–0.83**; run `farol calibrate` on your own history.
The details per language are in docs/how-it-works.md, and the reasons behind every choice in
docs/DECISIONS.md.

## Security and privacy

- `analyze` **never executes code** of the analyzed repository and **never uses the network**. The Go and Python helpers use only their standard libraries and only parse.
- Only `comment` (GitHub API) and `usage` (Datadog API) talk to the network. Error messages are not copied from Datadog, only error types.
- In CI the job that runs your code has no secrets and no write token; the job that comments never runs your code.
- Shadow mode: farol informs, it never approves, requests changes or fails a check.

## Limitations

- Static reading: values built at runtime are invisible (computed route paths, `getattr`, `importlib`, DI containers, registries filled in loops). When an entry point cannot be read, the PR is `unknown`; when a call cannot be resolved, farol assumes it reaches more, never less.
- TypeScript frontends: React Router, Next.js and TanStack Router (file-based) only: no code-based TanStack route trees, Remix/React Router file conventions, Vue or Svelte. JavaScript files, renamed files and TypeScript backends use module-level reach.
- Go: route prefixes from middleware stacks other than chi/gin/echo groups are not applied, and project types that wrap a router with their own registration API (Gitea's `web.Router`) are not read. Python: Django REST Framework routers are not read.
- The score and verdict thresholds are heuristics checked on a few repositories. Calibrate them on yours.

## FAQ

**We already have an AI reviewer. Why add farol?** They answer different questions. The agent comments on the lines
in the diff; after it, farol tells the person who approves how risky the merge is and which files carry the risk, from
static analysis of the whole program. Run both: farol's comment and report sit next to the agent's, and neither blocks
the merge.

**Is it free?** Yes. farol is open source under the MIT license, with no account, hosted service or paid tier: run it
with `npx @winninjs/farol` or the GitHub Action `winnin/farol/action`.

**Will it slow down CI?** No. farol runs after your tests and reuses their reports. The analysis takes about 3 s for
a 300-file Python service, 8–10 s for a large TypeScript monorepo or a Go service with a cold cache, and under a
second for the base when its helper output is cached.

**Can I use it outside GitHub?** Yes. `analyze`, `html` and `report` work anywhere; only `comment` is
GitHub-specific. Post the output of `npx @winninjs/farol report` with your platform's API.

**The report says "not verified".** That report was not given, or the path is wrong. Paths given to `analyze` are
relative to the current directory; paths in `farol.config.json` are relative to the project.

**A page I changed is not listed.** Run `npx @winninjs/farol routes` to see the entry points farol reads, and
`npx @winninjs/farol impact `
to see what reaches a file. Unreadable route constructs are listed under diagnostics.

**Go: "farol reads Go modules offline: run go mod download".** The module cache lacks a dependency of the base or the
head. Run `go mod download` for both before analyzing.

**Monorepo?** Point `--cwd` at the app. Paths stay relative to the repository root, and changes in apps the project
does not use are listed as outside it.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome: route adapters, frameworks, languages, report formats and better heuristics. See
CONTRIBUTING.md for the setup, the architecture and the conventions, and
SECURITY.md to report a vulnerability.

## License

MIT © 2026 Winnin

title: Show HN: Find overlapping Rust tests with mutation testing
author: yasuyuky
body:
To tackle the ever-increasing number of tests, I built cargo-test-prune.The idea behind it is to use cargo-mutants to generate mutants, and then solve the set cover problem for those mutants to suggest which tests can be eliminated.
(use a greedy algorithm to cover the detected mutants with fewer tests)I came up with this as a countermeasure against the monotonically increasing tests that tend to accumulate, especially when coding with AI.In fact, this very repository was also written using AI.I ran this tool on a previous revision of this repository. There were 11 tests and 108 generated mutants: 73 were caught by the tests, 23 survived, and 12 failed to compile.
I removed the 5 tests suggested by the tool and re-ran the same 108 mutants. The remaining 6 tests caught the exact same 73 mutants.Tests partly serve as documentation, so simply applying this isn't necessarily recommended, but since writing less code still holds value in the AI era, I think this tool could be quite useful.

title: Show HN: Shrinking my 159-byte x86-64 Hello World ELF to 153 bytes
author: michidk
body:
Skip to main content Hashnode Michi's Blog 
Back to My Website Back to My Website 
 Search Ctrl K ⌘K Toggle theme Write Open menu 
Smallest "Hello World" continued
 Updated October 10, 2026 · 13 min read · Markdown 
M Michael Lohr 
On this page
 Loading the first syscall number directly Loading the message's address directly Loading the message length directly Pushing the syscall number onto the stack Never fail Settling the bill Failing gracefully, for free On to new waters What about Zig? 
Nearly two years ago, I wrote about the smallest possible "Hello World!" program . It's one of my most read blog posts. Recently, I started playing around a lot with AI (like almost everybody else), so I thought: let's fact-check my previous blog posts! Turns out I was wrong: I actually did not create the smallest possible 'Hello World' program!
Buuut, I was pretty close! To summarize the rules of this challenge:
runs on modern 64-bit x86 Linux
executes directly, without a separate program or decompression step
is a proper, specification-compliant executable
keeps instructions outside the ELF header and program headers
prints Hello, World!\n (14 bytes) to stdout and exits with status 0
My previous result: 159 bytes (or 121 bytes in the 32-bit version). How did I get there? Using assembly and manually constructed ELF headers. These rules are important, as people have gotten as small as 77 bytes by hacking the ELF header. That example also needs five-level paging and permissive memory-overcommit settings, so it doesn't run on every modern x86-64 Linux machine. Header instructions aren't automatically invalid ELF, which is why I'm explicitly excluding them here.
My previous solution—can you spot what's wrong with it?
https://gist.github.com/michidk/aaf08c7678e02b574973556d0fba741e 
Codex Astra found a better solution that was able to reach 153 bytes .
Loading the first syscall number directly
To print the message, I first put the write syscall number, 1 , into rax . My original version used push 1; pop rax , which takes 3 bytes .
But in this directly loaded static Linux executable, rax starts at zero: it receives the successful exec return value. So we only need to change its lowest byte!
While eax is a 32-bit subregister of the 64-bit rax , there is another one: al is the lowest 8 bits of the rax register, so just one byte (= 8 bits, duh)! The constant also fits in one byte, making mov al, 1 just 2 bytes long.
; Before: 3 bytes
push 1
pop rax
; After: 2 bytes
mov al, 1
That's 1 byte saved . It relies on Linux's startup behavior, which is fine for our Linux-specific challenge. It isn't a general guarantee for an entry point reached through some other loader.
Loading the message's address directly
I used lea to calculate a pointer to the message bytes and put it into the lower 32 bits of the rsi register, which is the register the write syscall expects for its buffer pointer. It calculates the address from the instruction pointer plus a relative offset and requires 6 bytes to encode the assembly instruction.
By using mov instead, I directly embed the address as a 32-bit constant, only taking up 5 bytes (1 byte less). This works because my executable loads at the fixed address 0x400000 , so the message's address is known and fits within 32 bits. Writing esi also clears the upper half of rsi , producing the correct 64-bit pointer. The exact address isn't special, but it needs to be fixed and fit within 32 bits. The original lea esi also truncates its result to 32 bits.
; Before: 6 bytes
lea esi, [rel msg]
; After: 5 bytes
mov esi, msg
Loading the message length directly
For the message length, I used another stack operation: push 14; pop rdx , taking 3 bytes .
Linux also starts rdx at zero in this executable. So, just like with rax , we can set only its lowest byte. That byte is called dl .
; Before: 3 bytes
push 14
pop rdx
; After: 2 bytes
mov dl, 14
This takes 2 bytes , saving another byte! The rest of rdx stays zero, leaving the whole register equal to 14.
These initial register values come from Linux's ELF initialization . Our program doesn't have a dynamic loader that could change them before our code runs.
Pushing the syscall number onto the stack
To exit the application gracefully, one calls the exit syscall, whose number is 60 . For that I used mov eax, 60 , which takes up 5 bytes .
Instead of using mov , one can also push that number onto the stack and then just pop it into the rax register. push can encode the small constant with a one-byte immediate, taking 2 bytes . pop rax adds 1 byte , setting the entire register to 60 and restoring the stack pointer within just 3 bytes .
That saves 2 bytes , though it accesses the stack. Unlike mov al, 60 , it remains correct even if the preceding write syscall returned a negative error code.
; Before: 5 bytes
mov eax, 60
; After: 3 bytes
push 60
pop rax
Wait, didn't we previously replace push and pop with mov ? Yes! At startup, we knew the registers were zero. After write , rax contains the syscall's return value. Different starting values, different optimizations.
Nice! There is another improvement, though:
Never fail
We can shave off one more byte from exactly that piece of code we just optimized. But it's a bit hacky:
; Before: 3 bytes
push 60
pop rax
; After: 2 bytes
mov al, 60
Just like mov al, 1 , this instruction is only 2 bytes long. This time, though, we need the preceding write to leave the upper bits of rax at zero.
This works when write succeeds and returns 14. Linux puts 0x000000000000000E into the whole rax register, so all its upper bits are zero. Replacing its lowest byte with 60 then leaves rax equal to 60. In fact, any return value from 0 to 255 would work this way, although only a complete 14-byte write prints our whole message.
However, if write fails, the raw syscall returns a negative error code whose upper bits are set. Changing only al leaves an invalid syscall number in the low 32 bits, which Linux uses to dispatch the call. Linux rejects that syscall with -ENOSYS , so our program continues past its final instruction and, in this executable, causes a segmentation fault.
Is this compliant with our rules, though? I'd say yes, if we explicitly assume that stdout accepts all 14 bytes in one successful write. If it can't accept our message, we can't print the required "Hello World" anyway. With the original startup code, we'd need the 156-byte version to also exit with status 0 after a returned write error. But we'll fix that below without adding any bytes! Neither version retries partial writes.
Settling the bill
So with all five changes, we are down to 153 bytes for the 64-bit version! Three one-byte savings in the setup for write , plus another three bytes saved in the setup for exit : 159 − 1 − 1 − 1 − 2 − 1 = 153 .
Here's the final 64-bit version, including the improved exit setup explained below:
https://gist.github.com/michidk/a2d048a126956ec4f6cf335f9782c37a 
The 32-bit version gets even smaller: 114 bytes , down from 121! It already used mov for the pointer, but the startup tricks work here too: mov al, 4 for write , mov dl, 14 for the length, and a one-byte inc ebx to turn the initial zero into stdout's file descriptor, 1. Two one-byte xchg instructions prepare exit(0) even after a returned write error. Unlike the 64-bit version, the exit syscall number is already 1, so we don't need another mov al ! The 32-bit version is a separate comparison and needs Linux's 32-bit compatibility support. You can find it here .
Of course, this doesn't prove that we've reached the absolute minimum. More assumptions, more bytes saved!
Failing gracefully, for free
We got smaller, but our exit setup still depends on write succeeding. Can we fix that without making the program bigger? Turns out, yes!
So far, we've only looked at setting the exit syscall number. But exit also needs an exit status in edi . Our code used xor edi, edi to set it to zero: XORing a value with itself makes every bit zero. This takes 2 bytes and also clears the upper half of rdi . Together with mov al, 60 , that's 4 bytes to prepare exit(0) .
Linux also starts rbx at zero, and our program never changes it before this point. Meanwhile, edi still contains 1 , the stdout file descriptor. The write syscall preserves those registers.
Meet xchg , short for exchange! It swaps the values of its two operands. So xchg eax, ebx puts the old value of ebx into eax and the old value of eax into ebx , without needing a temporary register. These swaps don't access the stack or memory.
There's also a handy encoding trick: when one of the registers is eax , x86 has a special short form. Both xchg eax, ebx and xchg eax, edi take just 1 byte each!
We can use those two instructions to swap our values into place:
; Before: 4 bytes
mov al, 60
xor edi, edi
; After: 4 bytes
xchg eax, ebx
xchg eax, edi
mov al, 60
The first exchange puts zero into eax and moves write 's return value into ebx . The second puts 1 into eax and zero into edi , which is our exit status.
Now rax has a known value again, so mov al, 60 safely sets it to 60. This works even when write returned a negative error code! The exchanges write 32-bit registers, which also clear their upper halves.
Each xchg takes just 1 byte , and mov al, 60 takes 2 bytes . That's the same four bytes as our previous exit setup. We stay at 153 bytes , but no longer need the successful-write assumption for the exit syscall. We still need a complete write to print the whole message, of course.
On to new waters
In the last post, we also wondered what the smallest Rust and Zig versions would be.
The answer is not that easy.
The safe version is:
https://gist.github.com/michidk/8af37f2f21a943522b35110857ae76d5 
With 4,506,168 bytes (about 4.3 MiB ) on Rust 1.98.1 , compiled directly with rustc and no optimization flags, this is quite large! That only counts the executable; its shared system libraries aren't included.
But if we allow assembly, we can just use Rust as a wrapper and write our own assembly inside Rust. Furthermore, we want to use no_std (so no Rust standard library), use no_main , and define our own entry point _start , as well as calling Linux syscalls to help reduce the overhead:
https://gist.github.com/michidk/0addb0fdcb7de291033027e742f44522 
Can we use our new assembly tricks here too? Yes! We make _start a naked function with #[unsafe(naked)] and put the entire instruction sequence in naked_asm! . That gives us control over every instruction: Rust doesn't add a function prologue or epilogue, so Linux's initial register values reach our assembly untouched. Rust documents naked assembly here .
This one takes up 1,616 bytes without size optimizations. It still needs -Cpanic=abort , -Crelocation-model=static , -Clink-arg=-nostartfiles , and -Clink-arg=-static , so these aren't completely default compiler flags. Static relocation lets us embed the fixed message address, and static linking keeps the dynamic loader from changing the initial registers before our code runs. This unoptimized build uses Rust's default LLD selection.
It also uses our two xchg instructions, so a returned write error no longer breaks the exit syscall!
But we can further get this down to 209 bytes by playing around with the compiler flags.
These measurements use Rust 1.98.1 , with GNU ld 2.47.20260726 for the optimized builds. Other compiler and linker versions might produce different sizes.
The Cargo.toml settings control compilation:
opt-level = "z" optimizes for small code rather than maximum speed
panic = "abort" disables panic unwinding, which this build requires
strip = "symbols" removes symbol names and debugging information
lto = true lets LLVM optimize across crate boundaries
codegen-units = 1 keeps the crate in one compilation unit, giving the optimizer more visibility
We also want to set the following rustflags in .cargo/config.toml :
https://gist.github.com/michidk/86cd97a26c4fe05638340ba9bf8a485c 
Save that gist's config.toml as .cargo/config.toml .
-Cforce-unwind-tables=no avoids forcing the generation of stack-unwinding metadata
-Crelocation-model=static generates code suitable for fixed addresses rather than position-independent loading
-Clinker-features=-lld disables Rust's automatic LLD selection. On our machine, this selects GNU ld, whose layout and options produced the measured result
The next two options are passed through -Clink-arg :
-nostartfiles skips the usual C startup objects. Our program supplies _start itself
-static prevents linking against shared libraries. Since this program needs no external libraries, it also avoids dynamic-loader machinery
The long -Wl,... argument forwards these comma-separated options to GNU ld:
--build-id=none omits the build-identification note
-z noseparate-code allows code and read-only data to share a load segment, avoiding extra headers and page-alignment padding
-z nosectionheader omits the section-header table. Linux can execute the file using its ELF and program headers
--no-eh-frame-hdr omits the unwind-information search header and its program-header entry, but doesn't by itself remove all unwind data
With these files in place, cargo build --release produces the 209-byte version. The settings apply to the release profile, so an ordinary cargo build won't produce this size.
We can even supply our own linker instructions to arrive at 153 bytes :
https://gist.github.com/michidk/dce89c57c0837fb89c81211bad7fcb64 
Save it as minimal.ld and enable -Clink-arg=-Wl,-T,minimal.ld in the rustflags array.
The script removes the 56-byte PT_GNU_STACK program-header entry and keeps the complete headers, code, and message together without overlapping them. This also drops explicit stack-permission metadata. No custom packer or post-link trimming needed!
What about Zig?
In Zig 0.17.0 , we can achieve something similar by setting a few custom parameters (see build-zig.sh ) and using the same linker script:
https://gist.github.com/michidk/743dc2b06fc3cdc95ab06604111f1a65 
This version has no handwritten assembly and uses Zig's standard-library syscall wrappers. It results in 157 bytes and still exits with status 0 after a returned write error.
Why can't we apply the same tricks here? Those wrappers initialize their syscall registers explicitly. The compiler doesn't know that Linux supplies zero initial values for this particular entry point, and ordinary Zig code can't directly ask for mov al , mov dl , or those register exchanges. So this version stays at 157 bytes . The same tricks can't be transplanted into our Rust versions without handwritten assembly, either: their dynamic loader, startup code, and library calls don't preserve the kernel's initial register state.
But if we allow inline assembly ( hello-inline.zig ), we can use callconv(.naked) and apply all the same tricks! That gets Zig down to 153 bytes with our linker script, or 209 bytes with GNU ld's default script. Zig documents naked functions here .
The Rust and Zig assembly versions now use the same instruction sequence as our handwritten 64-bit version: 19 bytes of instructions , plus the 14-byte message and 120 bytes of ELF headers . All three reach 153 bytes , and all three still exit with status 0 after a returned write error. Nice!
You can find all the files and build instructions here .

---

## README

# edgepad

Touchpad edge gestures for Linux/Wayland.

`edgepad` turns touchpad edges into command zones while keeping normal pointer movement on the center of the pad. Swipe from an edge to run commands such as changing workspaces, opening a launcher, or sending desktop notifications.

The hard part is input correctness: Type-B multitouch slots, mixed edge/center contacts, `SYN_DROPPED` recovery, and virtual touch cleanup are covered by replay tests before they touch real hardware.

## Features

- Edge gestures on the left, right, top, and bottom touchpad zones.
- Continuous edge sliders for stepwise controls such as volume and brightness.
- Normal touchpad passthrough for unclaimed center contacts.
- Long-running user-session daemon with TOML config.
- Transactional config reload without releasing the touchpad grab.
- Command actions as argv arrays, without shell re-splitting.
- Automatic touchpad discovery when exactly one readable candidate is present.
- Read-only device discovery and capture tools for debugging.
- Bounded live proxy mode for testing real hardware.
- Nix package, NixOS module, Home Manager module, release installer, and systemd user service.

## Core concepts

The touchpad is split into four edge zones: `left`, `right`, `top`, and `bottom`.

- A **gesture** runs one action when the finger lifts. It can match either a directional swipe or a
 tap.
- A **tap** is a gesture whose contact never leaves the configured movement tolerance.
- A **slider** runs repeated steps while the finger moves, which is useful for volume or brightness.
- An **action** is the command that edgepad starts for a gesture or slider step.

A slider and a tap gesture can share the same edge. A slider and a directional gesture cannot,
because both would need to own the same movement.

## Install

### Release installer

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/assembledev/edgepad/main/install.sh | sh
```

Preview the install plan first:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/assembledev/edgepad/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --dry-run
```

The release installer is the complete setup for an x86_64 Linux desktop with systemd. It downloads
a static binary, installs the udev rules, writes a default config to
`~/.config/edgepad/edgepad.toml`, installs and starts the user service, then runs `edgepad doctor`.
It asks for `sudo` only when installing the udev rules.

### Update

Run the same installer command again. It keeps your config, replaces the installed files, restarts
the daemon, and checks that the service is healthy.

### Uninstall

Uninstall files created by the release installer:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/assembledev/edgepad/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall
```

This keeps `~/.config/edgepad/edgepad.toml`. To remove the config too:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/assembledev/edgepad/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall --purge
```

### Nix

For normal desktop use, install both the NixOS module and the Home Manager module. The NixOS module
provides device access; the Home Manager module owns the config and user service. See the complete
Nix setup.

The commands below only build or run the package. They do not install device rules or a user service.

Build and run from the repository:

```bash
nix build .#edgepad
./result/bin/edgepad --help
```

Run without installing:

```bash
nix run github:assembledev/edgepad -- --help
nix run github:assembledev/edgepad -- devices
```

## Quick start

The config installed by the release script uses desktop notifications as safe example actions.
Gestures will show what they matched, but they will not change your volume, brightness, media state,
or workspace until you replace those commands.

Check that the service, config, and touchpad are ready:

```bash
edgepad status
```

The service becomes active only after the virtual touchpad is created and the physical device is
grabbed. Status output includes the ready daemon's PID, version, and selected device when systemd
provides them.

If status reports a problem, run the full check:

```bash
edgepad doctor
```

Edit your config:

```bash
$EDITOR ~/.config/edgepad/edgepad.toml
```

Example config:

```toml
device = "auto"
edge_width = 0.10
tap_min_duration_ms = 40
swipe_min_distance = 0.02

[[sliders]]
zone = "left"
up = ["notify-send", "edgepad", "volume-up"]
down = ["notify-send", "edgepad", "volume-down"]

[[sliders]]
zone = "right"
up = ["notify-send", "edgepad", "brightness-up"]
down = ["notify-send", "edgepad", "brightness-down"]

[[gestures]]
zone = "top"
direction = "tap"
action = ["notify-send", "edgepad", "play-pause"]
```

Reload the user service after config changes:

```bash
systemctl --user reload edgepad.service
```

The daemon validates the complete file and keeps the previous configuration if the reload fails.
If a touch is active, it defers the swap until all fingers lift, so one contact is never interpreted
using two configurations. Changing the configured input device still requires a service restart.

Watch logs:

```bash
journalctl --user -u edgepad.service -f
```

If pointer input behaves incorrectly, stop edgepad immediately:

```bash
systemctl --user stop edgepad.service
```

The physical touchpad is ungrabbed when the daemon stops. Start it again with:

```bash
systemctl --user start edgepad.service
```

For a foreground run, `edgepad daemon` reads `~/.config/edgepad/edgepad.toml` by default.

## Gesture config

`device` can be `"auto"` or an explicit event node:

```toml
device = "auto"
# device = "/dev/input/event7"
```

`edge_width` is the fraction of the touchpad reserved for edge zones on each side:

```toml
edge_width = 0.10
```

Individual edges can optionally override that default. Omitted overrides continue to use
`edge_width`:

```toml
left_edge_width = 0.08
right_edge_width = 0.12
```

`tap_min_duration_ms` ignores very short edge taps. It defaults to `40`; set it to `0` to disable the guard.

```toml
tap_min_duration_ms = 40
```

`swipe_min_distance` is the minimum normalized touchpad travel that turns an edge contact into a
directional gesture. It defaults to `0.02`, or 2% of the corresponding touchpad axis. Smaller
movement remains a tap, so the same physical gesture behaves consistently across coordinate ranges.
Once a contact reaches this distance it no longer qualifies as a tap, even if it returns to its
starting point. A slider contact that emits any steps is also consumed by the slider and does not
emit an additional tap when released.

```toml
swipe_min_distance = 0.02
```

Each gesture binding has a zone, direction, and action:

```toml
[[gestures]]
zone = "top"
direction = "right"
action = ["notify-send", "edgepad", "top-right"]
```

Zones:

```text
left, right, top, bottom
```

Directions:

```text
up, down, left, right, tap
```

Continuous controls use `[[sliders]]`. Side zones use vertical `up`/`down` steps; top and bottom zones use horizontal `left`/`right` steps. `step` is normalized touchpad travel and defaults to `0.04`.

```toml
[[sliders]]
zone = "left"
step = 0.04
up = ["pamixer", "-i", "3"]
down = ["pamixer", "-d", "3"]
```

Slider zones can share the same edge with `tap` gestures, but not with directional `[[gestures]]`.

Actions are argv arrays. They are not run through a shell, so write shell logic explicitly when needed:

```toml
action = ["sh", "-c", "date >> /tmp/edgepad-actions.log"]
```

For desktop commands, prefer running `edgepad` as a user service so actions inherit the user session instead of root's environment.

## How it works

`edgepad` reads the physical touchpad, claims contacts that begin in configured edge zones, and forwards unclaimed contacts through a virtual touchpad.

For live forwarding it:

1. opens the physical touchpad;
2. reads the device's multitouch capabilities;
3. creates a virtual touchpad through `/dev/uinput`;
4. grabs the physical device;
5. routes edge contacts to the gesture recognizer;
6. emits normal contacts through the virtual device;
7. releases virtual contacts and ungrabs the physical device on shutdown.

The output side does not blindly copy raw pointer-emulation events. `BTN_TOUCH`, `BTN_TOOL_*`, and legacy `ABS_X/Y` are synthesized from unclaimed passthrough contacts so an edge-owned finger does not leak into normal pointer movement. Physical touchpad buttons (`BTN_LEFT` and related pointer buttons) are passed through, and live mode preserves input properties such as `INPUT_PROP_BUTTONPAD` so libinput keeps clickpad behavior.

On a buttonpad/clickpad, a physical button press takes priority over edge recognition. Active edge-owned contacts are promoted to normal passthrough contacts before the button event, and remain passthrough until they lift, so physical clicks and click-drag work even inside configured edge zones. This cancels the pending edge gesture; slider steps already emitted are not rolled back. Tap-to-click does not produce a physical button event, so an edge tap keeps the normal edge-gesture behavior. Touchpads with separate buttons keep independent edge and button handling.

## Permissions

`edgepad` needs access to:

- the physical touchpad event node under `/dev/input/event*`;
- `/dev/uinput` for virtual touchpad output.

The preferred desktop setup is a user service with logind/uaccess ACLs. The NixOS module and release installer install udev rules for that mode.

Manual commands that read real input devices may need `sudo`, the `input` group, or active seat ACLs. Use `edgepad doctor` to see what your system is missing.

## Troubleshooting

Start with these two commands:

```bash
edgepad status
edgepad doctor
```

Common problems:

- **More than one touchpad was found:** run `edgepad devices`, then set an explicit
 `device = "/dev/input/eventX"` in the config.
- **The touchpad or `/dev/uinput` is not accessible:** use the access fix reported by
 `edgepad doctor`. If udev rules or group membership just changed, start a new login session.
- **The service stays in `activating`:** edgepad is still waiting for a readable touchpad or
 `/dev/uinput`. Check `edgepad doctor` and the service log.
- **An action command is missing:** install that program, use its full path, or replace the example
 action with a command available on your desktop.
- **Pointer input is wrong:** stop the service with `systemctl --user stop edgepad.service`, then
 inspect `journalctl --user -u edgepad.service -b`.

## Diagnostics and capture

`proxy`, `replay`, and `replay-raw` use the normal edgepad config. Pass `--config ` to use
another config, or `--built-in-defaults` to ignore it.

Device discovery is read-only:

```bash
edgepad devices
edgepad devices --all
```

Capture recognizer-level events from a real touchpad:

```bash
edgepad dump --device auto --out bug.ev --frames 300
edgepad replay bug.ev
```

The frame count is a minimum capture budget. If it is reached while a finger is down, dump asks you
to release all contacts and records their release frames before exiting.

Stop `edgepad.service` before capture: the running daemon holds the physical touchpad with
`EVIOCGRAB`, so another reader receives no events. `dump` warns after three seconds without input
but never stops the service automatically. If input arrives later, it confirms that capture has
started and records it normally.

Capture raw evdev events for passthrough/output debugging:

```bash
edgepad dump --raw --device auto --out bug.raw.ev --frames 300
edgepad replay-raw bug.raw.ev
```

Inspect live routing without forwarding input:

```bash
edgepad proxy --device /dev/input/eventX --frames 300 --dry-run
```

Run a bounded live virtual-touchpad proxy test:

This command grabs the physical touchpad for the duration of the test. Normal pointer input is sent
through edgepad's temporary virtual touchpad until the frame limit is reached.

```bash
edgepad proxy --device /dev/input/eventX --frames 300 --uinput --grab
```

If auto-detection finds multiple touchpads, use the event node reported by `edgepad devices`. If the
OS denies access to the event node or `/dev/uinput`, run `edgepad doctor` and use the access model it
reports for your system.

## Commands

```text
edgepad devices     List readable input devices and touchpad candidates
edgepad status      Show a short daemon/config/device summary
edgepad doctor      Check config, runtime prerequisites, actions, and service health
edgepad daemon      Run the live edge-gesture proxy
edgepad dump        Capture touchpad events into a replay fixture
edgepad proxy       Run a bounded live proxy session for diagnostics
edgepad replay      Replay a parsed fixture through the recognizer
edgepad replay-raw  Replay a raw evdev capture through routing and output composition
```

## Documentation

- Device discovery
- Dump capture
- Passthrough and uinput
- Replay fixture format
- Nix

## Development

Clone the repository and enter its development shell:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/assembledev/edgepad.git
cd edgepad
nix develop
```

Build and check the project from there:

```bash
cargo build --locked
cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --locked
```

## Contributing

Feedback, issues, and pull requests are welcome.

How the split is worked out
Start from the UK totals for each area of spending in 2025-26 (£1227.9bn across ten areas of public services). For the six areas where HM Treasury can attribute spending to a nation (2024-25), each total is scaled by how much more or less is spent per resident in England than the UK average. The results are put back to 100%, and your income tax plus National Insurance is shared out in those proportions. Debt interest is shown separately from the rest of general public services.

What this does and does not show
Your tax is not tied to any one service. Everything is paid into one pot, so a proportional split is an illustration of where the pot goes.
Income tax and employee National Insurance are only part of what the government collects. VAT, corporation tax, council tax, employer National Insurance and other taxes also pay for these services, and the government borrows to cover the gap between spending and receipts.
Total managed expenditure was £1360.1bn in 2025-26. About £132bn of that is accounting adjustments that are not spending on any service, so the shares use the £1227.9bn spent on the ten areas.
Spending by nation: HM Treasury only attributes some spending to a nation (2024-25). Defence, debt interest, other public services, environment and culture are shared across the UK and are not adjusted. Per-resident figures from 2024-25 are applied to earlier and later years too, so treat the nation differences as a guide. Your tax is not ring-fenced to your own nation.
Wales and Northern Ireland use the same income tax bands as England. Only Scotland sets its own bands for earnings. Welsh income tax rates are the UK rates, with the UK government rate reduced and the Welsh Government adding the same amount back.
Student loan repayments come off your take-home pay but are not tax. They go to the Student Loans Company to pay off your loan, so they are left out of the spending split. Payroll works them out each pay period and rounds down, so your payslips may differ by a few pounds.
The calculator ignores pension contributions, benefits in kind, savings and dividends. Use HMRC's own tools for your exact bill. This is an estimate, not tax or financial advice.
Frequently asked questions
 Where does my income tax go?
 Income tax and National Insurance go into one pot that pays for public services. The largest areas are social protection (benefits and pensions, about a third), health (about a fifth), debt interest, education and economic affairs such as transport. Enter your salary above to see your own split in pounds.
 What is the UK Personal Allowance in 2026/27?
 The standard Personal Allowance is £12,570, the amount you can earn before paying income tax. It reduces by £1 for every £2 of income above £100,000 and is zero at £125,140. It is the same for 2024/25 and 2025/26.
 How much National Insurance do employees pay?
 For 2024/25 to 2026/27 the Class 1 employee rate is 8% on earnings between £12,570 and £50,270 a year, and 2% above £50,270.
 Is income tax different in Scotland?
 Yes. Scotland sets its own income tax bands on earnings, with six rates from 19% to 48%. Wales and Northern Ireland use the same bands as England. Select where you live above to see the difference, or see tax by salary in Scotland .
 How much student loan will I repay?
 You repay 9% of your earnings above your plan's threshold, or 6% for a Postgraduate loan. For 2026/27 the yearly thresholds are £26,900 for Plan 1, £29,385 for Plan 2, £33,795 for Plan 4, £25,000 for Plan 5 and £21,000 for Postgraduate loans. Plan 5 repayments start in April 2026. If you have a Postgraduate loan as well as another plan, you repay both. Pick your plan above to see the amount and your take-home pay.
 Which tax year does this tool use?
 You can choose 2026/27, 2025/26 or 2024/25. Spending figures are from HM Treasury outturn data for 2025-26 and 2024-25, and every source is linked at the bottom of the page.

title: Show HN: Hindsight – Lightweight, elegant, open-source tracker for Windows/macOS
author: Tomotsugu-dev
body: Hi HN, I’m building Hindsight, a free, open-source activity tracker for Windows and macOS.I know there are plenty of time trackers. I wanted something that combined automatic tracking, detailed charts, and cross-device sync in a lightweight app with an interface I enjoyed using. I couldn’t find a free option that fit, so I started building my own.Hindsight records active apps and window titles while it’s running, without requiring you to start and stop timers. You can explore your activity through daily, weekly, and monthly charts, drill down into individual apps and window titles, and use a yearly heatmap to spot patterns. Categories are customizable.There’s also an optional screenshot and OCR feature for finding something you previously saw on screen. Both are off by default. When enabled, you can search recognized text and jump back to the corresponding screenshot.The AI features can generate daily summaries or answer questions about your activity, with links back to the underlying records so you can check the answers. You can use a local model or connect a cloud API; third-party API fees may apply.Optional sync through Google Drive or WebDAV lets you view activity from Windows and Mac devices separately or together. I’ve also recently added plugin support so other developers can extend the app.I’d appreciate feedback, particularly on how you’d want to explore your activity history. What would make this useful to you beyond simply showing how many hours you spent in each app?Happy to answer questions about how it works.

title: Show HN: Independent Vet – Find locally owned vets (and corporate ones) near you
author: packeted
body: Three years ago, our dog was sideswiped by a car and my wife took him to the local vet in Berkeley. Unfortunately, things did not go well and to cut a long story short, he passed after 2 days and $13k of bills for very limited care. I was surprised to learn that the seemingly mom & pop practice had been acquired by a PE-owned consolidator and that around 50% of practices in the US are now owned by mostly PE-backed corporate groups - a trend that rapidly accelerated after COVID.I started a small janky passion project called https://privateequityvet.org which used Leaflet.js to map corporately owned veterinary practices in the US. The site gradually took off, was covered on PBS Newshour and now gets 20k uniques a day.A few months ago I launched IndependentVet.com which aims to be the opposite of the original site, helping pet parents in the US/Canada/UK identify locally owned veterinary practices. Just yesterday I launched native mobile apps that I developed over the course of three intense weeks of evenings and weekends using Opus 5.5. While it's early days, I'm really happy with how it turned out: https://independentvet.com/getWould love to hear what you think!

DADGPT Costume

4. Open DADGPT. People walk up, talk to Dad, or get roasted.

Why won’t skeletons fight each other?

Your browser hears you. A language model writes one pun. Dad says it out loud.

## Snap. Roast. Burn.

Roast me.

Nice vampire cape. Shame the only thing it scares off is dates.

Tap the camera. Dad counts down, snaps a photo, and roasts what he sees. Photos are never saved.

Vector files print sharp at any size. The PDF fills a letter page.

## Make your own Dad

Paste this into Claude Code or any coding agent. It sets up DADGPT with your own keys.

```
Set up my own copy of DADGPT, the dad joke costume app at https://github.com/johnpolacek/dadgpt. Read the README first.

1. Clone it and install with pnpm. It needs Node 24.
2. Copy .env.example to .env.local. Ask me for my Anthropic API key and a passcode to lock live mode. An OpenAI key is optional and gives Dad a better voice.
3. Run pnpm dev. Open /live and confirm Dad answers out loud with a joke, and that the camera button roasts a photo.
4. Deploy it to Vercel with the same environment variables, then give me the URL.

## Video Demo

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/19bec26d-6e01-4ee0-906e-7e69bace2f9c

## Key Features

- **Rearrangeable layout** where every key is its own 1u PCB
- **CH32V003** RISC-V microcontroller on every key
- **STM32WB55RGV6** main board with Bluetooth and USB
- **Pogo pins on all 4 sides** of every key for power and I2C
- **Magnetic cases** to hold the modules together
- **Key programming** from the main board over pogo pins
- **2MB QSPI flash** (W25Q16JV) to store the key firmware
- **Battery charging** with the BQ25895 and solder pads for a 1S LiPo
- **Buck-Boost converter** (TPS631000)
- **RGB status LED**
- **USB-C** with ESD protection
- **Ceramic Bluetooth antenna**

## PCB

Designed in KiCad! There are two boards, the Keybit and the Keyword, and both are 1u (19.05mm x 19.05mm).

### Keybit

A single key with a Cherry MX switch and a CH32V003. Every side has pogo pins for 3.3V, GND and I2C so it can connect to the keyword or to other keybits, and the pads on the corners are for programming.

### Keyword

The main board that the keybits connect to. It is split into two PCBs that stack on top of each other. The top one has the STM32WB55RGV6, the antenna and the flash, and the bottom one has the USB-C, the charger and the buck-boost converter. The 3 pogo pins on the top are for programming the keybits.

 About Jag's AI Heat Map
An interactive map of the AI companies, models, products, people, hardware and ideas that are getting the most attention in AI news and developer communities. Bigger, closer to the centre and more connected means more talked about.
Browse the articles
The Articles button (top right) opens a scrollable archive of every article behind the map — the last 90 days, grouped by source, newest first. Pick a source on the left to see just its stories; click any headline to open it in a new tab. The small red number under the button counts how many new articles were discovered in the last hour.
How heat works
Every story adds heat to each entity it mentions, weighted by source and popularity (Hacker News points, Hugging Face upvotes, GitHub stars). Heat cools with a 24 -hour half-life , so the map reflects the last few days of a 7-day window. Links join entities that appear in the same stories. Week covers 7 days with a 24-hour half-life; Today covers 24 hours with a 6-hour half-life and compares with 6 hours earlier. Breaking (orange name, pulsing ring) means an entity got at least 2 stories and 2.5× more attention in the last 6 hours than in the 6 hours before. New (orange ring) marks entities first spotted this week; ↑ means heat is at least 1.5× what it was 24 hours earlier, ↓ that it has cooled. Topics are drawn as diamonds; the hottest topic is filled orange and its closest connections are outlined.
