Subsurface Scattering and Performance Capture Pipelines in Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014)
October 24, 2026 by CodeAIHQ 
 Achieving absolute anatomical fidelity and tangible physical weight within a digital creature and set simulation pipeline demands uncompromising control over dynamic skeletal kinematics, multi-layered epidermal shaders, and volumetric light diffusion. In Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014), director Matt Reeves and the technical supervisors at Weta Digital discarded conventional computer graphics overlay shortcuts, establishing a rigorous hardware-to-simulation architecture that grounds digital primates inside uncompressed, real-world outdoor environments. Rather than relying on static digital geometry, the production deployed advanced portable motion-capture rigs, markerless machine-learning tracking algorithms, and finite element muscle deformations. This calculated methodology forces digital mass to interact organically with natural terrain and atmospheric physics frame-by-frame, successfully generating a heavy, undeniable sense of biological realism directly on the cinematic lens sensor.
Sub-millimeter tracking: Translating human micro-expressions into complex primate facial topologies through advanced head-mounted camera arrays. In this technical visual effects breakdown, we deconstruct the ruggedized hardware tracking frameworks that eliminate the uncanny valley, analyze the volumetric subsurface scattering matrices that dictate skin translucency, examine the finite element muscle simulation architecture used to calculate physical tension, and dissect the fluid integration pipelines that bind digital mass to environmental moisture and organic debris.
 1. Outdoor Performance Capture and Markerless Facial Tracking Systems
 The core technical foundation of the film’s unprecedented character authenticity stems from the deployment of custom uncompressed dual head-mounted camera (HMC) rigs paired with hybrid markerless tracking classifiers. While historical industry workflows restricted performance capture to controlled indoor volume stages equipped with static infrared markers, Weta Digital engineered ruggedized hardware capable of sustaining extreme outdoor exposure without signal degradation across rain, mud, and fluctuating natural daylight conditions.
 Sub-Millimeter Mesh Deformation and Retargeting Matrices
 This environmental freedom necessitated a sophisticated approach to high-frequency mesh deformation and skeletal retargeting across divergent primate chassis. The pipeline processed raw actor micro-expressions directly into precise corrective blendshapes, mapping human muscular ranges of motion onto complex chimpanzee and gorilla bone structures. Furthermore, dedicated infrared tracking isolated precise eye convergence vectors and pupil dilation, ensuring that subtle psychological subtexts transferred seamlessly into the underlying digital armature without procedural jitter or synthetic smoothing.
 By bypassing traditional painted facial markers, the engineering team eliminated tracking data loss caused by heavy perspiration during high-intensity physical sequences. The convolutional neural networks processed micro-movements in real-time, translating the subtle twitch of a lip or the tightening of a brow into accurate digital displacements that mirrored the exact emotional intent of the human performers.
Environmental mobility: Deploying uncompressed portable capture rigs to record organic actor kinematics directly within unstructured natural terrain. 2. Advanced Subsurface Scattering and Epidermal Layer Simulation
 Rendering believable digital skin exposed to unpredictable natural lighting required a complete departure from traditional flat texture mapping. Weta Digital implemented proprietary physically based rendering (PBR) shaders driven by multi-layered dipole and multipole subsurface scattering (SSS) approximations. Light penetration was computed not as a surface bounce, but through volumetric biological simulation across distinct dermal strata:
 Stratum Corneum Interactivity: Captured high-frequency specular highlights, sweat accumulation, and forest condensation across the outer skin barrier.
 Epidermal Melanin Distribution: Modeled variable pigmentation density, governing how deeply light penetrated before scattering back outward with translucent vitality.
 Dermal Diffusion Matrices: Calculated internal vascular dispersion, blood flow attenuation, and subcutaneous tissue density beneath the muscular framework.
 Simultaneously, the fur simulation engine managed over three million individual hairs per character, dynamically recalculating index of refraction (IOR) values whenever rain or mud saturated the pelage. This caused uniform light absorption and darkened albedo levels to match true biological physics, preventing the synthetic look common in earlier digital creature features.
Biological translucency: Multi-layered dipole subsurface scattering algorithms simulating light diffusion, melanin density, and moisture across digital primate skin. 3. Kinetic Muscle Simulation and Environmental Interactivity
 Beyond skin fidelity, the physical mass and momentum of the characters required an advanced mechanical simulation of internal anatomy. Utilizing finite element methods (FEM), the muscle pipeline computed real-time tension, compression, and skin sliding mechanics whenever an ape lunged or brachiation forces occurred. These volumetric muscle fibers pushed organically against the skin, generating realistic wrinkles, bulging veins, and flesh folds that responded instantly to gravity vectors, wet foliage, and continuous collision detection algorithms.
 The fluid dynamics integration further enhanced environmental realism by tracking droplet adhesion, run-off vectors, and absorption rates across both fur and skin surfaces. When characters waded through rivers or emerged from heavy rainfall, particle-based fluid solvers managed water runoff with absolute physical consistency, ensuring that every movement maintained correct mass distribution within the digital space.
 Deconstructing this complex biological pipeline demonstrates that definitive visual effects masterpieces achieve permanent industry status when uncompromising technical engineering overrides conventional computer graphics shortcuts. Through the precise integration of portable hardware capture, multi-layered epidermal shaders, and advanced finite element anatomical modeling, the production established an enduring benchmark for digital character performance and realistic cinematic world-building.

title: Show HN: A client-side adaptive cognitive test measuring micro-hesitations
author: mr-boombastic
body:
Hi HN!
I’m not a software engineer by trade. My background is in behavioral science and human-computer interaction, but I wanted to solve a specific problem I found when applying for jobs which is the logical test. They are booooring, easy to cheat on if you really want to and provides very limited information about people. I built this prototype from scratch sing AI to bring my idea to life.
So now I've been working on this side project for a Cognitive Adaption Engine (CAT/KAT in swedish) for about three weeks. Many pre-employment screening tests i've done use a static item bank and are very liberal with the time allowed on each question, making it easy for Vision LLMs or bots to beat. 
I wanted to see if I could build a fast, client-side engine (JS/SVG) that combats this problem by measuring certain biometric cognitive signatures like "switch cost" (how long it takes for your brain to re-adjust when logical rules change) and "post error-slowing". 
To go beyond the simple grading of correct/incorrect, this test dynamically gives you waves of patterns/challenges through a local item bank based on your millisecond response times. If you use an LLM, the constant latencies gets punished with a lower score. If they use a script, the complete lack of natural human variance will be picked up on.
I am currently trying to calibrate a baseline and need high-aptitude users to stress-test it and to provide more data. It also makes it very fast to complete.Everything runs 100% locally in your browser and since I did use AI, I would love your feedback on how the architecture holds up and the technical approach to anti-cheating or anything that comes to mind on this topic.(Optional) When you finish the test, you can press Ctrl + Shift + X on the results page which unlocks a hidden admin console. There you can see more info on your performance and even download a HR-pdf that translate your data into three tailored interview questions. Unfortunately the admin page is in Swedish, but I believe you will get the idea.

comments.author: mr-boombastic
comments.text: I should also add that this isn't supposed to replace the traditional g-factor test, but used as a supplement to gain more information about the candidate!

So now I've been working on this side project for a Cognitive Adaption Engine (CAT/KAT in swedish) for about three weeks. Many pre-employment screening tests i've done use a static item bank and are very liberal with the time allowed on each question, making it easy for Vision LLMs or bots to beat. 
I wanted to see if I could build a fast, client-side engine (JS/SVG) that combats this problem by measuring certain biometric cognitive signatures like "switch cost" (how long it takes for your brain to re-adjust when logical rules change) and "post error-slowing". 
To go beyond the simple grading of correct/incorrect, this test dynamically gives you waves of patterns/challenges through a local item bank based on your millisecond response times. If you use an LLM, the constant latencies gets punished with a lower score. If they use a script, the complete lack of natural human variance will be picked up on.
I am currently trying to calibrate a baseline and need high-aptitude users to stress-test it and to provide more data. It also makes it very fast to complete.Everything runs 100% locally in your browser and since I did use AI, I would love your feedback on how the architecture holds up and the technical approach to anti-cheating or anything that comes to mind on this topic.(Optional) When you finish the test, you can press Ctrl + Shift + X on the results page which unlocks a hidden admin console. There you can see more info on your performance and even download a HR-pdf that translate your data into three tailored interview questions. Unfortunately the admin page is in Swedish, but I believe you will get the idea.

title: Show HN: Tributary – Discover who influenced your favorite musicians
author: ASpring

title: Show HN: WhatsApp Bridge for those with their own VPS
author: vid_t
body:
# vid-t/whatsapp-bridge Self-hosted, read-only bridge to your WhatsApp chats, with an MCP server and a web admin UI built on top of whatsmeow - Stars: 2 - Forks: 0 - Watchers: 2 - Open issues: 1 - License: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 - Default branch: main - Created: 2026-10-24T09:37:35Z ## Languages - CSS - Dockerfile - Go - HTML - JavaScript - Shell - TypeScript ## Topics - claude - golang - mcp - mcp-server - model-context-protocol - self-hosted - whatsapp - whatsmeow ## Top Contributors - vid-t (12 contributions) --- ## README # whatsapp-bridge **A self-hosted bridge & seutp gateaway built on top of whats-meow for storing and accessing your raw whatsapp data** CI Licence: AGPL-3.0-only whatsapp-bridge links to your WhatsApp as an extra device, the way WhatsApp Web does. It keeps the chats you choose in an encrypted database on your own VPS, where you can serach the chats or query them using MCP. For now, it is read only. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR phone["Your phone
(WhatsApp)"] -- "linked device,
like WhatsApp Web" --> bridge["whatsapp-bridge
on your server"] bridge --> db[("Encrypted database
messages of ticked chats only")] ai["Your AI assistant
Claude · ChatGPT · Codex"] -- "MCP, after you sign in
read-only tools" --> bridge ``` 1. **Link.** On your phone, open **Settings › Linked devices › Link a device** and scan the QR code. The bridge now receives your messages like any other linked device in WhatsApp. 2. **Tick.** Choose only which chats it keeps. Every chat starts unticked, and the bridge stores none of its messages until you tick it. Tick within an hour of linking to also keep the history WhatsApp sends at linking. 3. **Ask.** Connect your assistant to `https:// /mcp` and sign in. It searches and reads your ticked chats when it needs to, and cites every message it uses. ## Try it locally Go 1.27 or newer. The web UI is built into the binary. ```sh git clone https://github.com/vid-t/whatsapp-bridge.git && cd whatsapp-bridge CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o bin/whatsapp-bridge ./cmd/whatsapp-bridge ./bin/whatsapp-bridge keygen > whatsapp-bridge.env && chmod 600 whatsapp-bridge.env ./bin/whatsapp-bridge serve -env-file whatsapp-bridge.env ``` Open, enter the access code from `whatsapp-bridge.env`, link WhatsApp and tick your chats. Tick them within the hour to keep their recent history. > [!IMPORTANT] > `whatsapp-bridge.env` holds the database key. Without it the database cannot be read, so > back it up. ## Run it on a server claude.ai and ChatGPT reach the bridge from their own servers, so they need a public HTTPS address. Claude Code and Codex also work over `localhost` or a private network. `deploy/SELF-HOSTING.md` has three paths. Each ends at `https:// ` with automatic HTTPS from Caddy. | Path | Best for | |---|---| | **A. cloud-init** | a fresh VPS: paste one file and boot | | **B. Docker Compose** | a server that already runs Docker | | **C. Install script** | an existing Ubuntu 24.04 or Debian 12 server | You need a domain pointing at the server, with ports 80 and 443 open. ## Connect your assistant In Claude Code: ```sh claude mcp add --transport http whatsapp-bridge https:///mcp claude mcp login whatsapp-bridge ``` In claude.ai, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT or Codex, add `https:// /mcp` as a connector and sign in on the page that opens. `docs/MCP-SETUP.md` has the steps for each assistant, plus API keys for scripts. Your assistant gets six read-only tools: | Tool | What it does | |---|---| | `search_messages` | full-text search across the ticked chats | | `read_chat` | read one chat in time order | | `get_message_context` | show the messages around a search hit | | `list_chats` | list the ticked chats, most recent first | | `get_document` | give the file name and caption of an attachment | | `get_status` | show the linked devices and how fresh the data is | Every message comes with a `wa://` citation, so you can check the source of an answer. ## Privacy and safety - **Read-only.** The code has no way to send messages, an "online" status or read receipts. The tools cannot change or delete anything. - **Only ticked chats.** Chats start unticked. The bridge never stores the messages of an unticked chat, only its name and last activity for the chat list, so no assistant can see it. For an hour after you link a phone, it holds those messages in memory only, so a chat you tick in that hour keeps its history. Then they are dropped. - **Encrypted at rest.** The database file is encrypted with Adiantum when `BRIDGE_DB_KEY` is set (`keygen` creates it). A running bridge decrypts messages in memory, so run it on a machine you control. - **Closed by default.** It listens on `127.0.0.1` and refuses a public address unless an access code and a database key are set. - **Audited.** Every tool call is logged: who called it, which tool, which chats and how many rows. The log never holds message text. - **Nothing goes to an AI provider on its own.** Your assistant gets messages only when it calls a tool, and only that call's results. - **Your phone stays in charge.** Unlink the device in WhatsApp and the bridge is cut off at once. WhatsApp also logs out linked devices when the phone has been offline for 14 days. > [!WARNING] > **Unofficial client.** whatsapp-bridge uses whatsmeow, > an unofficial implementation of the WhatsApp Web protocol. It is not affiliated with, > endorsed by or connected to WhatsApp or Meta. WhatsApp does not permit unofficial > clients, and an account linked to one can be restricted. Staying silent and read-only > keeps that risk low but cannot remove it. You accept it when you link an account. **Not built yet:** downloading attachments and reading their text, and limiting what each member sees (today every member sees all ticked chats). ## Documentation - Configuration and commands: every setting, flag and command - Self-hosting: install, upgrade and back up - Connect your assistant: Claude, ChatGPT, Codex and API keys - Security policy · Contributing ## Licence AGPL-3.0-only. If you run a modified whatsapp-bridge as a service, you must offer its source code to the people who use it. Error fetching https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugin_asdk_app_6abdec89d46c81919cda058ca9f62cb8?search=call4me: CRAWL_EMPTY_CONTENT

title: Show HN: Perch, a calm Mac app for juggling Claude Code sessions
author: eastandwestwind
body: I'm an engineer, but I also hate using tools that make things overcomplicated.It's also tough with the new pace of AI-driven development to really get into the flow state, and maintain (still needed!) focus on 1 thing.So I built a tool that I actually want to use every day.Curious if others would find this useful, too, or have any feedback? Like if it's nearly there, what changes would make this a win for your workflow?Details:- It's a Mac app (Apple Silicon) that runs your Claude Code sessions side by side. Each piece of work gets a "context" with its own session, next steps, status, PRs, and links.- The dashboard groups contexts by whose move it is: yours, waiting on a reviewer or teammate, Claude working, or idle. You get a notification when a session needs you or a PR gets review comments.- For non-engineers, there's a Chat view instead of the terminal, a guided Claude Code install, and folder pickers instead of paths. Engineers can stay in the real Claude Code terminal.- It runs the actual claude CLI, and sessions keep running if you quit Perch. You can also import your existing Claude Code sessions.- Everything stays on your Mac. There's no account and no analytics, and crash reports are opt-in.

comments.author: A1kmm
comments.text:
Any exploit might be interactive with a backend component that generates and serves payload components based on interactive responses.OP (and anyone else who exploits the server) would be able to see the transcript between the backend and the vulnerable server, containing the payload customised for the server, but not the actual code of the backend. This would be useful if it was a 0day vulnerability, but with a disclosed vulnerability getting a payload that doesn't work except on their server, without the code that generated it, might not be that much value over what they already have.That said, there are other ways to scam by structuring things like the OP (none of this should be taken to imply the OP has actually done this, but rather why this structure as a general approach might be a bad idea):* This could be a 'stone soup' scam where the OP has the wallet keys (obviously), and puts this up to bait the addition of more funds into the wallet by other interested people. The key might not actually even be on the server, or it might not be vulnerable. Once sufficient other people add funds, the OP could withdraw the funds, recouping their original funds plus anything others added.
* This could be run as a propaganda scam either to falsely sell that it isn't an easily exploitable vulnerability when it is (by making it unreasonably difficult to exploit compared to real-life deployments), or to over-inflate how exploitable it is (by an insider withdrawal from the wallet). Manipulating public opinion could allow an attacker with a working exploit more time, or help to sell services to fix the problem.I think an alternative scheme that is less vulnerable to scams would be to have a ZKVM (Risc0 or similar) executing vulnerable code, such that the attacker needs to produce a zero knowledge proof transcript of getting the ZKVM into a particular state that would not be possible if they didn't have an exploit. It should also take an Ethereum address as a public input. Then write an Ethereum contract that will allow funds to be transferred to the public input Ethereum address if submitted with a valid proof transcript, and back to the source of funds after some time has passed. Everyone who wants to add to the jackpot could deploy their own version of the contract, so the one proof transcript could claim from all of them, but if unclaimed the funds go back to the source.Alternatively (avoiding the risk exploits may be so large as to make the cost of producing the proof transcript impractical), they could be built using a public cloud provider's trusted computing offering (e.g. Google Confidential VMs). The person making the challenge could make it so the derivation (NixOS for example) to produce the entire image executing on the cloud provider in a deterministic way (with publicly known source, and hash codes of each stage publicly available). Then, from the code with the known hash, they use the vTPM to generate an attestation that a key was generated while the vTPM PCRs were in a known state (corresponding to the publicly reproducible hashes), and ensure the only way to access the key from the instance is via an exploit. It would also include logic to generate and wrap a Bitcoin wallet key, and emit the public key (with the attestations and a signature linking back via a vTPM attestation to the cloud provider's key). This way, unless the cloud provider is also in on the scam, people could be assured that the OP isn't scamming them.

title: Show HN: Wasi-Python – CPython, NumPy, and Pandas in a WebAssembly Sandbox
author: clay-gendron
body:
# ClayGendron/wasi-python

A statically linked CPython for WebAssembly hosts (wasm32-wasip1) with numpy, pandas, scipy, and more compiled in. Built for running untrusted agent code server-side in web applications.

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 0
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Homepage: https://claygendron.github.io/wasi-python/
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-16T16:52:04Z

## Languages

- C
- C++
- Dockerfile
- Fortran
- LLVM
- Python
- Rust
- Shell
- WebAssembly

## Top Contributors

- ClayGendron (1175 contributions)
- claude (86 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

**A secure Python sandbox for agent-generated code with the scientific stack inside.**

wasi-python is CPython 3.15 compiled to WebAssembly as one static binary. It includes numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, statsmodels, matplotlib, and forty plus other packages.

It is built to run code that AI agents generate, or any other code that is untrusted and must be kept apart from the host process. By default, the sandbox sees no host files and has no network access.

Run it from Python with one `pip install`, or load the same binary into any WebAssembly host that supports exception handling.

# Installation and Quick Start

```
$ pip install wasi-python
$ wasi-python run -- -c "print('hello, WebAssembly')"
{"exit_code": 0, "fuel_used": null, "stderr": "", "stdout": "hello, WebAssembly\n", "trapped": null, "truncated": []}
```

Requires Python 3.11 or later. The wheel carries the runtime, which unpacks to about 250 MB of WebAssembly and bytecode, so nothing else is downloaded. Every release is tested on Linux (x86-64 and arm64), macOS (arm64) and Windows (x86-64). Install says more about what comes with the package and where it keeps its cache.

# Usage

### 1. The Scientific Stack in a Sandbox

Run numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas inside a Python sandbox. The following recovers a frequency from a noisy signal with numpy, fits a curve with scipy, clusters points with scikit-learn and summarises them with pandas.

```python
from wasi_python import run

code = """
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import optimize
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

t = np.linspace(0, 5, 200)
signal = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3 * t) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, t.size)
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(t.size, d=t[1] - t[0])
print(f"dominant frequency: {freqs[np.abs(np.fft.rfft(signal)).argmax()]:.1f} Hz")

(a, k), _ = optimize.curve_fit(lambda t, a, k: a * np.exp(-k * t), t, 3 * np.exp(-0.7 * t) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, t.size))
print(f"decay fit: a={a:.2f} k={k:.2f}")

points = np.vstack([c + rng.normal(0, 0.5, (100, 2)) for c in ([1, 1], [5, 5], [1, 5])])
labels = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(points)
print(pd.DataFrame(points, columns=["x", "y"]).groupby(labels).mean().round(1))
"""

done = run(["-c", code])
print(done.stdout.decode())
```

```
dominant frequency: 3.0 Hz
decay fit: a=2.97 k=0.70
     x    y
0  5.0  5.0
1  1.0  0.8
2  1.1  5.0
```

`done` also carries `exit_code`, `stderr`, `fuel_used` and `trapped`, which names the limit that stopped a call, such as `"deadline"` or `"out of fuel"`. Results and errors describes every field, and Packages lists what each package can do inside the sandbox.

### 2. Safe and Secure by Design

The program inside the sandbox is the guest. Your program is the host. Make two folders on the host, each with a file. Grant the guest one of them, then watch it try the other, the parent folder and a write.

```python
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

from wasi_python import Grant, run

for name in ("wasi_python_shared", "wasi_python_private"):
    Path(name).mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (Path(name) / "hello.txt").write_text(f"hello from {name}\n")

code = """
for path in ("/shared/hello.txt", "/private/hello.txt", "/shared/../private/hello.txt"):
    try:
        print(path, "->", open(path).read().strip())
    except OSError as e:
        print(path, "->", type(e).__name__)

try:
    open("/shared/notes.txt", "w")
except OSError as e:
    print("write to /shared ->", type(e).__name__)
"""

done = run(["-c", code], grants=[Grant("wasi_python_shared", "/shared")])
print(done.stdout.decode())

shutil.rmtree("wasi_python_shared")
shutil.rmtree("wasi_python_private")
```

```
/shared/hello.txt -> hello from wasi_python_shared
/private/hello.txt -> FileNotFoundError
/shared/../private/hello.txt -> PermissionError
write to /shared -> PermissionError
```

Now ask the guest to reach the network.

```python
from wasi_python import run

code = """
import urllib.request

try:
    urllib.request.urlopen("https://pypi.org")
except Exception as e:
    print("network ->", type(e).__name__)
"""

done = run(["-c", code])
print(done.stdout.decode())
```

```
network -> URLError
```

And every call runs under limits. Here each limit is set low so you can watch it stop a call.

```python
from wasi_python import run

spin = "while True: pass"

done = run(["-c", spin], deadline_s=1)
print("deadline ->", done.trapped)

done = run(["-c", spin], fuel=50_000_000)
print("fuel ->", done.trapped, done.fuel_used)

done = run(["-c", "x = bytearray(512 * 1024 * 1024)"], memory_bytes=128 * 1024 * 1024)
print("memory ->", done.exit_code, done.stderr.decode().strip().splitlines()[-1])

done = run(["-c", "print('x' * 10_000_000)"], output_bytes=1_000_000)
print("output ->", len(done.stdout), done.truncated)
```

```
deadline -> deadline
fuel -> out of fuel 50000000
memory -> 1 MemoryError
output -> 1000000 ('stdout',)
```

Everything the guest can reach is something you handed it. It starts with no files, no network and no way to start a process. A folder comes in through a `Grant` and a host function through `tools=`, and nothing else gets in. Instructions, time, memory, output and open files each have a default cap, and when a guest hits one the call ends and the result says which. The guest is a WebAssembly module with its own memory, so it holds no pointer into your process, and its only calls into the host are the WASI functions and the tools you pass. Each release is built reproducibly and signed by the workflow that built it. Verify a download shows how to check one.

### 3. Bring Your Own Tools

The guest can call functions from your own program, as tools. Decorate a function, pass it in `tools=`, and guest code imports it with `from host import tools`. The guest sees the function's name, signature and docstring, so a model can read `help(tools)` and use it.

```python
from wasi_python import run
from wasi_python.tools import tool

PRICES = {"apple": 0.5, "pear": 0.8}

@tool(read_only=True)
def price(item: str) -> float:
    """Look up the unit price of an item.

    Args:
        item: The item's name, such as "apple".
    """
    return PRICES[item]

code = """
from host import tools

basket = {"apple": 6, "pear": 3}
print("total", sum(tools.price(name) * n for name, n in basket.items()))
try:
    tools.price("plum")
except Exception as e:
    print("plum ->", e)
"""

done = run(["-c", code], tools=[price])
print(done.stdout.decode())
```

```
total 5.4
plum -> price failed (internal error)
```

A tool runs with your program's authority, so hand the guest narrow functions rather than whole services. When a tool raises, the guest learns only that it failed. The traceback and its message stay on your side, in the call record at `done.tools`. A `gate=` function can look at every call before it runs and refuse it. Tools covers schemas, gating, the record, and recipes for LangChain and MCP tools.

### 4. Maintains State Across Turns

A `Session` keeps one interpreter across several calls, like a notebook kernel. Imports and variables carry over, and a final expression is echoed.

```python
from wasi_python import Session

with Session() as session:
    session.run("import numpy as np; x = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=10_000)")
    print(session.run("print(round(float(x.mean()), 3), round(float(x.std()), 3))").stdout.decode())
    print(session.run("int((x > 2).sum())").stdout.decode())
```

```
-0.011 0.998
216
```

A session ends when you close it, when it rests longer than `idle_s`, or when `lifetime_s` passes. Each turn gets its own fuel and deadline. Sessions covers what carries over, how a session ends, and the shutdown.

### 5. And Async Of Course

`run_async` is the async version of `run`. The guest runs on a worker thread, and guests run in parallel. Here three guests each sleep for a second while a task on the event loop keeps ticking.

```python
import asyncio

from wasi_python import run_async

async def ticker():
    for i in range(3):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
        print("event loop is free, tick", i)

async def main():
    guests = [run_async(["-c", f"import time; time.sleep(1); print('guest {n} done')"]) for n in range(3)]
    results, _ = await asyncio.gather(asyncio.gather(*guests), ticker())
    for done in results:
        print(done.stdout.decode().strip())

asyncio.run(main())
```

```
event loop is free, tick 0
event loop is free, tick 1
event loop is free, tick 2
guest 0 done
guest 1 done
guest 2 done
```

Cancel the task to stop the guest. `Session` has `run_async` too. Async covers cancellation, pool sizing and forking servers.

# What's Inside

| Artifact | What it is |
|---|---|
| `python.wasm` | a WASI reactor: CPython with numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, statsmodels, matplotlib, lxml and regex compiled in |
| `python-snapshot.wasm` | the same binary with the interpreter already started, for a faster first call |
| `python-stdlib.zip` | the standard library and the packages' Python code, as bytecode in one read-only zip |
| `MANIFEST` | every pinned source, toolchain and recipe hash the build used |

They are published as release assets on GitHub and inside the `wasi-python` wheel on PyPI. More on the artifacts.

Packages lists every package with its version and what works. Each package's own test suite runs inside the sandbox before a release.

There are no processes, no network and no `pip` inside the guest. Limitations lists every difference from native Python, each with its reason.

# Hosts

The binaries use WebAssembly's exception-handling proposal, so a host must support it. This project runs wasmtime 49 itself. The rest of this list is read from each runtime's release notes and source, not run here.

- **Runs by default:** wasmtime 47 or later (CLI, Rust, wasmtime-py); WasmEdge 0.16 or later.
- **Runs with a switch:** wasmer 6 or later on LLVM or V8, or 7 or later on Cranelift (not Singlepass); wazero 1.12 or later; Node 24.15 or later.

To bring your own host, install the files without wasmtime-py, `pip install --no-deps wasi-python`, and find them with `wasi_python.artifacts()`. Importing `wasi_python` never loads wasmtime. The `wasi_python` package enforces the limits in section 2. Another host sets its own. Embedding from other languages shows how.

# Build From Source

The build is one command from pinned inputs. Every source is fetched by URL and checked against its SHA-256 before use.

```
scripts/00_download.sh   # fetch every pin and verify it against downloads/SHA256SUMS
scripts/build.sh         # build the artifact set; logs in build/logs/
```

The source trees are the released tarballs plus a few recorded patches (upstream patches carried: 27), each offered upstream and dropped once upstream releases the fix. Building gives the full details.

# Contributing, Security, Changelog

- Contributing: start here. AGENTS.md is the rule book every change follows.
- Security policy: report a way out of the sandbox privately.
- Changelog: what each release changed.

# Agentic Development

`v0.1.0` was built by Claude Opus and Fable agents in six days of near-continuous work from October 16th to the 22nd of 2026. The agents made 1,255 commits across 421 sessions, had up to 12 working at once, and read 500 million tokens and generated 9 million. Every change was specified first, built in its own worktree, reviewed by a fresh agent and judged by the test suite before it landed. How it was built has the full account, with charts. The rules are in AGENTS.md and the contributing pages.

# Licences

wasi-python is licensed under Apache-2.0. The artifact set carries the licence of every component it links, one file each in its `LICENSES` folder. The wheel's `LICENSE` file holds the Apache-2.0 text followed by each of those licences.

  entry         files      size  share largest inside, without a row of its own
  ■ Pictures        910    1.0 GB    64% Screenshots 211 · 25-10-26-kappadokien.jpg ? · test 2 · kinoview-logo.png…
  ■ Downloads        23  574.4 MB    36% chatgpt_amd64.deb ? · Antigravity.tar.gz ? · Telegram Desktop 4 · Tiedote…
  ■ go              ~13 ~182.6 MB   ~12%
  ■ Documents     ~4.1k ~154.2 MB   ~10%
  ■ Recordings        4  533.0 kB    <1% meetings 4
  ■ bin              17   38.8 kB    <1% record-meeting ? · meeting ? · goal-loop ? · sandbox ? · tools 8 · worklo…
  ■ snap              2    3.7 kB    <1% libreoffice 2 · android-studio 0 · firefox 0 · firmware-updater 0 · gimp …
  ■ +10 smaller       0       0 B     0%
  partial: walk deadline 2s · not scanned 957

```

## What it counts

duls stays on the filesystem of the directory it inspects. A mount below it,
such as `/proc`, `/sys`, `/run`, a tmpfs `/tmp` or a second disk, is not
entered: its entries belong to that filesystem, so every total above it is a
lower bound and the footer counts it as `other filesystems N`. That keeps a
virtual file's apparent size out of the view: `/proc/kcore` reports 128 TiB
and stores nothing.

Sizes are apparent bytes, the size the filesystem reports for a file, so they
compare with `du --apparent-size -x`. Hidden entries are left out unless
`--all` is set and `du` counts them, so pass `-a` to compare like for like; on
a developer machine `.git`, `.cache` and `.local` are most of the tree. A line
count comes from a second pass over the files the view can show, bounded by
`-t`.

`df` answers a different question: it counts the blocks the whole device
allocates, including what no walk can reach. That is directories this user may
not read, mounts the walk leaves, the filesystem's own tables, and space no
name holds any more. When a run cannot reach the whole tree it states the
device beside its own totals, so the difference is visible instead of missing:
`filesystem 281.0 GB used of 501.8 GB`. duls prints SI bytes, so this figure is
about 7 % larger than `df -h`'s GiB column.

## Flags

The flags that change what duls shows or how long it takes. Run `duls -h`
for the complete list.

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| ----------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-a`, `--all` | off | Include hidden entries. |
| `-json` | off | Print the JSON document, whatever the stream. |
| `-t`, `--timeout` | `2s` | Run deadline; `0` removes it and the large-file count cap. |
| `--all-types` | off | Disable the extension deny-list when counting lines. |
| `-bytes` | off | Exact byte counts instead of SI units; visual view only. |
| `-r`, `--refresh` | `15m` | How long a stored line count stays trusted; `0` disables the cache. |

## Development

`AGENTS.md` is the developer guide and
`architecture/` holds the contract, one concern
per file. One solid rule:

```sh
make qa # lint plus the full Go test suite
```

must pass with exit code 0.

MIT, see LICENSE. The view, the palette, and the presentation are
extracted from slivingdoc by the same author.

## README

 
 
 

 AEON-CUT 

 
 Audio Silence & Breath Cutter for DaVinci Resolve 21 
 Powered by pure Rust (egui) GPU-accelerated interface and high-precision Voice Activity Detection (VAD).
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

---

 
 
 

---

## Highlights

* **100% Free & Open Source:** No monthly SaaS subscriptions ($10–20/mo saved).
* **Blazing Fast Native Rust GUI:** Built with `egui` / `eframe` — silky smooth 60+ FPS, instantaneous startup, and custom DaVinci Resolve dark studio aesthetic.
* **100% Local & Private:** No video or audio is ever uploaded to external servers or cloud providers.
* **Non-Destructive Editing (Handles Preserved):** All speech cuts preserve media references so edge handles can be trimmed or extended directly on the timeline anytime.
* **Multi-Language Support (i18n):**
 * 🇺🇸 English
 * 🇹🇷 Türkçe
 * 🇨🇳 简体中文
 * 🇯🇵 日本語

---

## Cutting Modes

1. **New Clean Timeline (Auto-Cut):**
 * Automatically creates a new timeline (`Timeline - AeonCut`) populated only with speech slices.
 * Switches Resolve's active viewer directly to the new timeline.
 * Silences are completely eliminated while keeping separate cut clips on Track 1.
2. **Append to Active Timeline:**
 * Appends the sliced speech clips directly onto your current working timeline.
3. **Add Clip Markers:**
 * Places non-destructive Cyan markers across speech and silence boundaries for manual review.

---

## Precision Controls

* **Silence Threshold (`dB`):** `-60 dB` to `-10 dB` (Default: `-32 dB`).
* **Min Silence Duration (`ms`):** Prevents cutting natural micro-pauses within sentences (Default: `350 ms`).
* **Start Breath Padding (`ms`):** Preserves the beginning consonant of words (Default: `120 ms`).
* **End Breath Padding (`ms`):** Softens the trailing edge of words (Default: `150 ms`).

---

## Quick Start

### Prerequisites

* Rust & Cargo (1.80+)
* Python 3 (3.6+)
* FFmpeg (Installed on system PATH)
* DaVinci Resolve Studio (21, 20, or 19)

### Running

```bash
git clone https://github.com/aethelisdev/aeoncut.git
cd aeoncut
cargo run --release
```

1. Open **DaVinci Resolve** and select a video/audio clip in your timeline.
2. In Aeon-Cut, click **"🔍 Analyze Clip"**.
3. Choose your cut mode and click **"✂ Apply Cuts to Resolve"**.

---

## Testing

Run automated Voice Activity Detection tests:

```bash
cargo test
```

## README

 Agensh: A Decentralized, Scalable Multiagent Harness 

 
 
 
 
 
 

### News

🚀 **2026-10-24:** We open-sourced **Agensh**, including the harness, experiment launch
scripts, and reproduction guide.

📢 **2026-09-22:** We published the **Agensh** preprint on arXiv.

## Overview

**Agensh is a self-organized multi-agent harness that scales to 1,024 agents.**
Agents discover and claim sub-tasks, share findings, verify results and
merge progress asynchronously, without a central orchestrator. A shared
workspace, message interface and shared context connect each agent's local
progress to the team.

We evaluated Agensh on the five hardest ProgramBench tasks
using GPT-5.6-sol with high reasoning effort, a six-hour budget and no Internet access.
Agents rebuild reference programs from behavioral observations and bundled
documentation. Across the 5 evaluated tasks, the mean final test-pass rate rises
from **19.31% with 1 agent** to **28.78% with 128 agents**, an improvement of
approximately **49% relative**. Larger teams also reach comparable pass rates
sooner. On **Pandoc**, the final test-pass rate rises from **33.89% with 1 agent**
to **50.94% with 128 agents** and **55.06% with 1,024 agents** under the same
six-hour budget. We find that self-organized peer coordination, integration
workflows and specialized roles gradually emerge as the team grows.

With the latest GPT-6.1-sol at high reasoning effort, the six-hour Pandoc test-pass
rate rises from **56.19% with 1 agent** to **79.59% with 32 agents**, a relative
improvement of **41.64%**.

Pandoc scaling results for GPT-5.6-sol and GPT-6.1-sol at high reasoning effort, with emergent coordination workflows and specialized roles

## Watch 1,024 agents work together

Animated replay of 1,024 agents cooperating through Gitea, Mattermost and shared context

## How it works

Agensh cooperation loop: gather context, claim a sub-task, take action, verify results and merge progress asynchronously through shared workspace, messaging and context

**Agensh defines the multi-agent cooperation loop.**
Workers concurrently gather context, claim sub-tasks, take action, verify results
and merge progress in a self-organized manner, repeating until the user’s goal
is achieved. All workers proceed asynchronously and share progress through the
infrastructure.
Gitea provides the shared workspace,
Mattermost provides the messaging interface, and the
shared context mechanism is adapted from DeLM.
In our experiments, we integrate Agensh on top of the per-agent agentic loop
of Copilot harness.

## Reproducing the experiments

This release includes a single-node team setup using Docker Compose and a
standalone single-agent baseline, both using native Copilot ACP sessions.

- Reproduction guide: prerequisites, configuration, image builds,
 launch commands, evaluation, recovery and release differences.
- Repository layout: component and folder guides.
- Team launcher and
 single-agent launcher: experiment entrypoints.

## README

# Argus

**The open-source security operations platform where AI agents do the legwork and you stay in control.**

Test
License: MIT

Argus watches your cloud, identity, code, endpoints, network and Kubernetes. It catches
attacks at machine speed, investigates them with AI agents, and contains them in seconds.
Every action is typed, checked against policy, dry-run first and reversible. It is
self-hosted, multi-tenant and MIT licensed, so your security data never leaves your hands.

Argus overview

## Why Argus

**Stop attacks while they are happening, not the next morning.** Autonomous response
playbooks act the moment a detection fires: block an attacker at Cloudflare, cut a laptop off
the network through CrowdStrike or SentinelOne, and more from a catalog of 27 typed actions.
They start in shadow mode so you can see what they would do, use only reversible actions,
stay within hourly and blast-radius caps, and roll themselves back unless you keep the change.

**Approve from Slack in one click.** Approve, deny or roll back actions straight from the
alert. No console, no context switch.

**AI that investigates without taking the wheel.** Seven specialist agents triage, investigate
and hunt using read-only tools. They can propose a fix but never execute one. Everything they
read is treated as untrusted data, so a prompt injection hidden in a log becomes a signal
instead of a hijack.

**See every AI tool your company is really using.** The AI gateway puts OpenAI and Anthropic
traffic behind org-held keys, model allowlists, data-loss prevention, prompt-injection flags
and budgets. Shadow-AI discovery finds the services people use without approval, using your
network, cloud and SSO telemetry.

**Catch rogue AI agents in the act.** Plant canaries built for agents: hidden prompt
injections, agent rules files, a fake MCP server and fake LLM API keys. Any agent that takes
the bait trips a detection, with its IP, model and prompt recorded.

**Prove your detections work before an attacker tests them.** The agentic attack simulator
replays 8 AI-driven attack scenarios in an isolated sandbox tenant, with optional evasion
variants, and reports exactly which ones you caught, which you missed and which rules were off.

**Pentest continuously, not once a year.** Autopilot has the red-team agent plan tests, runs
them through the scope-checked harness, and re-plans from what it finds. It only runs inside
scopes a human has marked for unattended testing.

**Fix what attackers are exploiting right now.** Every finding with a CVE is enriched with
CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list and EPSS exploit-probability scores, and severity
is raised automatically. It works offline for air-gapped installs.

**Audit-ready from day one.** A hash-linked, signed audit chain records every action, approval
and agent step, mirrored to S3 Object Lock or Azure immutable storage. Control mappings for
SOC 2, NIST 800-171 and ISO 27001 are included.

**Runs anywhere you do.** Docker Compose for a pilot, Helm for Kubernetes, and Terraform for
AWS and Azure. Every autonomous feature ships off by default, so you turn on exactly as much
autonomy as you trust.

This README describes what is in the repository today. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` describes the
design; `docs/ROADMAP.md` lists what is implemented versus planned.

## Project status

Argus is an open-source foundation, meant to be forked and extended. The platform core
(tenancy, auth, RBAC, audit chain, queue, policy and approvals) is tested end to end on SQLite
and PostgreSQL in CI. Tune collectors and detection rules to your estate, and start in
monitoring-only mode (`docs/GO-LIVE.md`) before enabling any action. It is not a certified
product; see `docs/COMPLIANCE.md` for what it can and cannot evidence.

## Architecture

```
  Browser / SDK / sensors
          |
          v  HTTPS (Caddy, ALB, Front Door or your ingress)
  +-------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  API  (FastAPI)  auth: session / OIDC+PKCE / TOTP / API keys |
  |  RBAC (viewer < analyst < operator < admin < owner), CSRF,   |
  |  per-principal rate limits, request ids, security headers    |
  +------+------------------+------------------+----------------+
         |                  |                  |
   PostgreSQL           Redis queue        Audit chain
   (tenant_id on       (leases, retries,   (hash-linked per tenant,
    every table)        python -m          HMAC, JSONL / S3 Object
                        app.worker)        Lock / Azure immutable)
         |                  |
  +------+------------------+----------------------------------+
  |  Worker processes run the same handlers as the API:        |
  |   collectors.run   detections.run / baselines              |
  |   graph.recompute  testing.run   agents.run                |
  |   autoresponse.evaluate   testing.autopilot                |
  |   simulation.run   intel.enrich / refresh   ai.discover    |
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
         |
         v  agents call propose_action only -> ActionRequest(pending)
  Action broker (separate policy, approvals, dry run, rollback, kill switch)
```

Trust boundaries, in one sentence each (details in `docs/THREAT-MODEL.md`):

1. Agents cannot execute anything; their one write-capable tool creates a pending request.
 Autonomous response acts only through the broker, as the system principal, with reversible
 non-critical actions, caps and automatic rollback.
2. Everything an agent reads is wrapped as untrusted data and the prompt says so.
3. Active testing runs only inside a recorded authorization and scope, re-checked at run time.
4. Every domain table carries `tenant_id`; queries go through a scoped helper; tests assert it.
5. The audit chain is hash-linked, HMAC-signed (required in production), and mirrored to an external, optionally WORM, sink.

## What is in this checkout

| Area | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|
| App factory, settings, DB, RBAC, auth (local, OIDC, TOTP, API keys), CSRF, rate limits | implemented, tested | `app/core/`, `app/api/auth.py`, `app/api/deps.py` |
| Audit chain with JSONL / S3 Object Lock / Azure immutable blob sinks | implemented | `app/core/audit.py` |
| Job queue (in-memory and Redis, leases, retries, cancellation, reaper) and standalone worker | implemented | `app/core/queue.py`, `app/worker.py` |
| Prometheus metrics, JSON logging, optional OpenTelemetry tracing | implemented | `app/core/telemetry.py` |
| Evidence graph: nodes, edges, attack paths, exposure scoring | implemented | `app/graph/`, `app/api/graph.py` |
| Detections: 13 rules (swarm x4, identity x2, cloud, k8s, code, canary, anomaly, agentic, unsanctioned AI service), baselines, canaries (12 kinds, 4 aimed at AI agents: planted prompt injection, agent rules file, fake MCP server, fake LLM key) | implemented | `app/detections/`, `app/api/detections.py`, `app/api/canaries.py` |
| Collectors: AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, GitHub, Okta, Entra, osquery, netflow | implemented with fixtures; cloud SDKs optional | `app/collectors/`, `app/api/collectors.py` |
| Test harness: scope policy, rate limits, adapters for web baseline, trivy, nuclei, zap, prowler, caldera, semgrep, gitleaks | implemented; tools must be installed separately | `app/testing/`, `app/api/tests.py`, `app/api/scans.py` |
| Agent runtime, providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, none), read-only tools, 7 specialists, eval suites | implemented | `app/agents/`, `app/api/agents.py`, `app/api/evals.py` |
| Action broker: catalog of 27 typed actions (AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, GitHub, Okta, Entra, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Argus-internal), policy, approvals, dry run, execute, rollback, kill switch | implemented | `app/actions/`, `app/api/actions.py` |
| Autonomous response: playbooks that act on detections without a human (shadow mode first, reversible actions only, caps, automatic rollback); Slack approve / deny / roll back buttons | implemented; off by default | `app/actions/autoresponse.py`, `app/api/autoresponse.py`, `app/api/slack.py`, `docs/AUTONOMOUS-RESPONSE.md` |
| AI gateway (governed OpenAI / Anthropic proxy: org-held keys, model allowlists, DLP, prompt-injection flags, budgets, usage log) and shadow-AI discovery from network, cloud and SSO telemetry | implemented; gateway off by default | `app/ai/`, `app/api/ai_gateway.py`, `app/api/ai_inventory.py`, `docs/AI-GATEWAY.md` |
| Autonomous pentesting: the red-team planner's plans are run through the scope-checked harness and re-planned from results | implemented; off by default, opt-in per tenant and per scope | `app/testing/autopilot.py`, `app/api/autopilot.py`, `docs/AUTOPENTEST.md` |
| Threat intel: automatic CISA KEV and EPSS enrichment of findings, offline cache | implemented | `app/intel/`, `app/api/intel.py`, `docs/INTEL.md` |
| Agentic attack simulator: 8 agent-driven attack scenarios replayed in an isolated sandbox tenant, coverage report, evasion variants | implemented | `app/simulator/`, `app/api/simulations.py`, `docs/SIMULATOR.md` |
| Integrations: 13 inbound parsers behind `POST /api/v1/ingest/{source}`, 6 outbound channels (webhook, Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, PagerDuty, email) with deliveries and retries, Wazuh indexer pull | implemented | `app/integrations/`, `app/api/ingest.py`, `app/api/integrations.py` |
| Admin, assets, findings, events, investigations, approvals, audit, reports routers | implemented | `app/api/` |
| Alembic migrations (4 revisions, through autonomy and AI security) and `scripts/migrate.py` | implemented | `alembic/`, `docs/MIGRATIONS.md` |
| Containers, compose, Helm, Terraform (AWS, Azure), CI, observability, docs | implemented | `Dockerfile`, `compose*.yaml`, `infra/`, `.github/`, `docs/` |

Routers are discovered automatically. The full v1 surface is in `docs/API.md`.

## Quick start (development, SQLite, no Docker)

Requirements: Python 3.11 or 3.12.

```bash
python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt
cp .env.example .env
python scripts/generate_secrets.py --write          # fills the three REPLACE_ values, plus AUDIT_SIGNING_KEY and DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY when they are empty
uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080 and sign in as `ADMIN_EMAIL` / `ADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`.
With `REDIS_URL` empty, jobs run inside the API process (`WORKERS_INPROCESS=true`). With
`DB_AUTO_CREATE=true` (the default) tables are created at startup; for Alembic-managed
schemas set it to `false` and run `python scripts/migrate.py` (see `docs/MIGRATIONS.md`).

Synthetic demo data in an isolated tenant (never touches the network):

```bash
python scripts/seed_demo.py
```

It prints a `demo` tenant login and creates DEMO-labelled assets, authorizations, events that
trip `cloud.public_exposure_change` and `swarm.machine_speed_sequence`, findings, a canary and
an agent run record. Refuses to run when `APP_ENV=production`.

Tests:

```bash
python -m pytest -q
```

## Pilot (Docker Compose: API, worker, PostgreSQL, Redis)

```bash
cp .env.example .env && python scripts/generate_secrets.py --write
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose logs -f api
```

`compose.yaml` binds the API to `127.0.0.1:8080` only, runs the API and worker from one image
with a read-only root filesystem, no capabilities and no Docker socket, mounts `./targets`
read-only, and applies the schema at API start (`RUN_MIGRATIONS=true`). Add
`--profile observability` for an OpenTelemetry collector, Prometheus (scraping `/metrics`) and
Grafana with the dashboard in `infra/grafana/argus.json`.

TLS termination for a single host:

```bash
# .env: APP_ENV=production COOKIE_SECURE=true BASE_URL=https://host ARGUS_DOMAIN=host ACME_EMAIL=ops@example.com
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d
```

## Production

Kubernetes: `infra/helm/argus` (API + worker deployments, HPA, PDB, default-deny
NetworkPolicy, ingress with TLS, optional ServiceMonitor). AWS: `infra/terraform` (ECS
Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, S3 Object Lock audit bucket, Secrets Manager, ALB + WAF).
Azure: `infra/terraform-azure` (Container Apps, Flexible Postgres, Azure Cache, immutable
blob container, Key Vault, Front Door + WAF).

The production checklist is in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`. The short version, enforced partly by
`assert_safe_config()` at startup:

- `APP_ENV=production` refuses to start without PostgreSQL, `REDIS_URL`, `COOKIE_SECURE=true`,
 an `https://` `BASE_URL`, `DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY(S)`, `AUDIT_SIGNING_KEY(S)`, an external audit
 sink, and either OIDC or `TOTP_REQUIRED=true`.
- Dedicated workers (`WORKERS_INPROCESS=false`, `python -m app.worker`).
- Use an object-lock audit sink (S3 Object Lock or Azure immutable blob), not only JSONL.
- `/metrics` blocked at the edge; egress filtering for workers; secrets in a secret manager.
- Images pinned by digest and verified with cosign (`.github/workflows/release.yml`).

## Roles

Roles are cumulative (`app/core/rbac.py`):

| Role | Adds |
|---|---|
| viewer | read everything in the tenant, including autoresponse playbooks and the AI inventory |
| analyst | edit findings and detections, run agents and evals, manage canaries, record approvals, use the AI gateway |
| operator | manage and authorize assets, run tests, scans, autopilot and collectors, request, approve, execute and roll back actions, run detections and simulations |
| admin | users, API keys, settings, collector and integration configuration, the actions kill switch, test scopes (including marking one autonomous), autoresponse playbooks, AI gateway policy |
| owner | tenant settings, approving critical actions |

API keys carry a role and optional scopes (for example `ingest`) that further restrict them.
A `system` principal is used only inside queue handlers.

## How agents, testing and actions are governed

**Agents** (`app/agents/runtime.py`). A specialist is an `AgentSpec` with a system prompt, a
list of tool names, an output schema and budgets (`AGENT_MAX_STEPS`, `AGENT_MAX_TOKENS`,
`AGENT_MAX_SECONDS`, `AGENT_COST_CEILING_USD`, with `AGENT_MODEL_PRICES` for models outside
the built-in Claude price table). Tools are read-only views over Argus data;
the only `propose` tool creates a pending `ActionRequest` through the broker. Every tool
result is redacted, truncated and wrapped as `<untrusted_data source=...>`; the guardrail
prompt tells the model that instructions inside evidence are indicators of injection. Each
model and tool step is persisted (`agent_steps`) with input hash, tokens and latency. With
`AI_PROVIDER=none`, specialists run deterministic fallbacks. Prompt-injection and precision
eval suites live in `app/agents/evals/suites/`.

**Testing** (`app/testing/`). A `TestScope` lists assets, allowed tiers (passive, active,
intrusive), environments, a UTC window, a rate limit and a concurrency limit (runs beyond
`max_concurrency` wait in the queue). A run is allowed only if
the asset has a current `AssetAuthorization` whose flags permit the tier, the scope permits
it, the window is open and the target passes policy validation. `scope.check()` runs at
request time and again inside the worker; intrusive tiers are limited to staging and lab
environments. External tools run through `run_tool()` with a fixed argv, a timeout, bounded
output and a minimal environment.

**Actions** (`app/actions/`). Typed actions declare risk, reversibility and a parameter
schema, and implement `dry_run`, `execute` and `rollback`. A request (from an operator or an
agent's `propose_action`) goes through policy (`app/actions/policy.py`: kill switch, tenant
`actions_enabled`, deny-lists, maintenance window, auto-approval only for low-risk reversible
actions when `ACTIONS_AUTO_APPROVE_LOW`), approvals (approver differs from requester; high risk
needs two when `ACTIONS_REQUIRE_TWO_FOR_HIGH`; critical additionally needs a principal with
`actions:approve_critical`), a dry run with blast radius, execution as the `actions.execute`
queue job with a stored rollback payload, and an audit entry at every transition.
`ACTIONS_KILL_SWITCH=true` (global, environment) or `POST /api/v1/actions/kill-switch`
(per tenant, sets `actions_enabled=false`) rejects every request and execution.

**Autonomy** (`docs/AUTONOMOUS-RESPONSE.md`, `docs/AUTOPENTEST.md`). Both autonomous features
need a global switch and a tenant opt-in, and both are off by default. Autonomous response
playbooks start in shadow mode (they record what they would have done), may only use
reversible, non-critical actions, are capped per hour and by blast radius, roll actions back
automatically unless a human keeps them, and ignore detections from the simulator. Autopilot
runs only in scopes a human has marked `autonomous`; the red-team agent plans, and every test
it proposes is re-checked by the normal scope machinery before and during execution.
`AUTOPENTEST_KILL_SWITCH` and the actions kill switch stop each one at once.

## Documentation

| Document | Content |
|---|---|
| `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` | design: packages, interfaces, data model, API table |
| `docs/API.md` | v1 route summary with status |
| `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` | dev, compose, Kubernetes, AWS, Azure; production checklist |
| `docs/AUTONOMOUS-RESPONSE.md` | autonomous response playbooks, safety limits, Slack buttons |
| `docs/AUTOPENTEST.md` | autonomous pentesting gates and how runs proceed |
| `docs/AI-GATEWAY.md` | AI gateway policy, DLP, budgets and shadow-AI discovery |
| `docs/SIMULATOR.md` | agentic attack simulator scenarios and coverage reports |
| `docs/INTEL.md` | CISA KEV and EPSS enrichment, caching and offline mode |
| `docs/MIGRATIONS.md` | Alembic workflow |
| `docs/GO-LIVE.md` | step-by-step production rollout in monitoring-only mode |
| `docs/SECURITY.md` | security model as implemented, reporting |
| `docs/THREAT-MODEL.md` | STRIDE per trust boundary, prompt injection, SSRF, tenancy, credentials, broker abuse, supply chain |
| `docs/RUNBOOKS.md` | incident procedures |
| `docs/COMPLIANCE.md` | SOC 2 / NIST 800-171 / ISO 27001 control mapping (evidence support, not certification) |
| `docs/ROADMAP.md` | implemented versus next |
| `CONTRIBUTING.md` | contributing guide |

## Security

Please report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting
(Security tab), not in public issues. Details in `docs/SECURITY.md`.

MIT for this repository. Third-party tools (nuclei, ZAP, Prowler, CALDERA, Semgrep, Gitleaks,
Trivy), cloud SDKs and model providers are governed by their own licenses and terms.
